islamic.text: Prophet Adam, peace be upon him, holds a revered position in Islam as the first human, the first prophet of Allah and the first Muslim; he is called Abu al-Bashar, "father of humanity". Allah fashioned him from clay, shaped him and breathed into him a soul (Sad 38:71–72). Allah told the angels that He would place a vicegerent (khalifa) on earth, and He taught Adam the names of all things; when the angels admitted they did not know them, Adam named them (Al-Baqarah 2:30–33). Allah then commanded the angels to prostrate before Adam (Al-A'raf 7:11), recognizing his unique honor and the knowledge bestowed upon him. Iblis refused out of arrogance, saying "I am better than him. You created me from fire and created him from clay" (Al-A'raf 7:12); he was cast out, becoming Shaytan, the accursed one, and vowed to mislead Adam's descendants. Adam was placed in Jannah (Paradise) with his wife Hawwa (Eve). The Quran says both were created from a single soul (4:1); the rib account comes from the Bible, and a hadith uses the rib as a metaphor. Allah permitted them to enjoy all its fruits but warned them against approaching a specific tree (Al-Baqarah 2:35). Shaytan, driven by envy, whispered that the tree would bring immortality (Ta-Ha 20:120), and Adam and Hawwa ate of it. Immediately recognizing their error, they repented: "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves" (Al-A'raf 7:23), and Allah mercifully accepted Adam's repentance (Al-Baqarah 2:37) — unlike Iblis, Adam sought forgiveness. They were sent down to Earth to live there for an appointed time (Al-Baqarah 2:36), and Adam guided his progeny towards the worship of the One God. The Quran tells of two of his sons, known in tradition as Qabil (Cain) and Habil (Abel), and of one killing the other (Al-Ma'idah 5:27–31). The Quran and authentic Sunnah do not state his age at death. According to a report cited by Ibn Qutayba, when he died the angels washed and shrouded him, Jibril led the funeral prayer, and they told his children, "This is your custom for your dead."
sources: Ibn Qutayba (report of Adam's funeral), via Wikipedia — Adam in Islam

christian.text: According to Christian scripture, specifically Genesis 2–3, Adam was the first human created by God. Formed from the dust of the ground, God breathed life into him, making him a living soul. God placed Adam in the Garden of Eden, entrusting him with its care and dominion over creation. Recognizing his need for a companion, God fashioned Eve from Adam’s rib, presenting her as his wife. They were commanded not to eat from the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil. Tempted by a serpent, Eve ate the forbidden fruit and gave some to Adam, who also ate. This act of disobedience, known as the Fall, introduced sin and death into the world, separating humanity from God. As a consequence, they were expelled from Eden. Adam then toiled the ground and fathered children, including Cain, Abel, and Seth. He lived 930 years, becoming the patriarch of all humanity, whose sin necessitated God’s plan of salvation through Christ. His life marks the beginning of human history and the entry of sin into creation, as understood in Christian theology.

jewish.text: Adam, the foundational figure in Jewish tradition, is introduced in the Torah, primarily in Genesis (Bereshit). Created by God from the dust of the earth and infused with the breath of life, Adam was the first human being, uniquely made in the Divine image. God placed him in Gan Eden, the Garden of Eden, instructing him not to eat from the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil. Adam was given the profound task of naming all living creatures, a demonstration of his intellectual capacity and dominion. Recognizing his need for companionship, God fashioned Chava (Eve) from Adam's rib, creating the first couple. However, their blessed existence was tragically altered when Chava, persuaded by the serpent, ate from the forbidden tree and offered it to Adam, who also partook. This act of disobedience resulted in their expulsion from Gan Eden, introducing labor, pain, and mortality into the human condition. Despite this, Adam and Chava began humanity’s lineage, raising children such as Kayin (Cain), Hevel (Abel), and Shet (Seth). Adam lived a total of 930 years, his life chronicled in Genesis as a pivotal account of creation, divine instruction, human choice, and the enduring consequences that define the human experience in Jewish thought.

bahai.text: Adam, revered in the Bahá'í Faith as the first in a succession of Divine Messengers or Manifestations of God, heralded the dawn of a new spiritual cycle for humanity. His coming, as elucidated in Bahá'í writings, marked a crucial turning point, initiating humanity's collective spiritual and social development. Bahá'í teachings do not interpret the biblical account of Adam as the literal first man created on Earth; rather, humanity had existed for eons prior to his advent. Instead, Adam represents the first in a long line of Divine Teachers sent by God to educate and guide humankind. The narrative of the Garden of Eden and the "fall" is understood symbolically. The Garden signifies the world of God, or the divine realm, while Adam and Eve represent the collective soul of humanity. The "tree of good and evil" symbolizes the material world or self, and the "fall" denotes humanity's descent from a state of pure spiritual unity into the complexities of the material realm, accompanied by the gradual unfolding of human consciousness. Through Adam, humanity received its initial spiritual laws and guidance, establishing the foundation upon which subsequent Manifestations, such as Noah, Abraham, Moses, Zoroaster, Buddha, Christ, Muhammad, the Báb, and Bahá’u’lláh, would build. His mission was to awaken spiritual awareness and civilize a nascent humanity, setting the stage for progressive revelation.

islamic.text: Prophet Idris, peace be upon him, is named in the Holy Quran in Surah Maryam and Surah Al-Anbiya. Allah says: "And mention in the Book Idris. Indeed, he was a man of truth and a prophet (siddiqan nabiyyan). And We raised him to a high station (makanan aliyyan)" (Maryam 19:56–57). In Surah Al-Anbiya he is named with Ismail and Dhul-Kifl, all of them steadfast and among the righteous admitted into Allah's mercy (Al-Anbiya 21:85–86). Islamic scholarship traditionally identifies him with the biblical Enoch. Islamic tradition places him among the earliest prophets, after Shith (Seth) and before Nuh (Noah): he is the second prophet named after Adam, in the line through Shith, and according to Ibn Kathir's Qisas al-Anbiya and al-Tabari's Tarikh he was the great-grandfather of Nuh and lived several generations before the Flood. Classical sources give no firm dates for him. He called his people to Tawhid, the worship of the One God, and away from idolatry. Tradition credits him with many firsts: he was the first to write with a pen, the first to study astronomy and the movements of the stars, the first to weigh and measure, and the first to sew and wear stitched garments; it also speaks of his knowledge of mathematics and other sciences, which he taught his community. The words "We raised him to a high station" gave rise to much commentary. Ibn Kathir reports traditions that Idris was taken up to the fourth heaven, where the Prophet Muhammad met him during the Mi'raj, as recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim. Other commentators read the "high station" as his exalted spiritual rank and closeness to Allah, not a physical ascent. Later Muslim mystical and philosophical writers linked him with Hermes: Ibn Arabi gave him a chapter, the Bezel of Holiness, in his Fusus al-Hikam, and earlier al-Mubashshir ibn Fatik and Abu Ma'shar al-Balkhi held that the first of three Hermeses was Idris, founder of philosophy, alchemy and the natural sciences.
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim (Mi'raj hadith, as cited in THE-O summary)

christian.text: Enoch (identified in Islamic tradition with Idris), an early patriarch in the lineage tracing from Adam to Noah, is a figure of profound faith within Christian scripture. Genesis 5 in the Christian Old Testament introduces him as the son of Jared and the father of Methuselah, noting his lifespan of 365 years. His most distinguishing characteristic, however, is the recurring statement that "Enoch walked with God." Unlike others in the genealogical record, Genesis 5:24 declares that "he was not, for God took him." This unique departure from earthly life is further expounded upon in Hebrews 11:5, which states, "By faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death; and was not found, because God had translated him: for before his translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God." This passage underscores his extraordinary faith and the divine intervention that spared him the experience of death, transporting him directly into God's presence. Additionally, the Epistle of Jude reveals Enoch as a prophet, foretelling the Lord's coming with "ten thousands of His saints, to execute judgment on all, to convict all who are ungodly among them of all their ungodly deeds which they have committed in an ungodly way, and of all the harsh things which ungodly sinners have spoken against Him." Enoch remains a testament to a life lived in intimate communion with God, culminating in a supernatural ascent.
sources: Bible, Genesis 5; Hebrews 11:5; Epistle of Jude

jewish.text: Enoch (identified in Islamic tradition with Idris), known in Hebrew as Chanoch, is a pivotal figure in the early genealogies of humanity, as recorded in the Torah, specifically Genesis 5. He was the son of Jared and the father of Methuselah, living an astounding 365 years. The biblical account provides a concise yet profound description of his life, distinguishing him among his contemporaries in the lineage of Adam through Seth. The central and most distinctive aspect of Enoch's life is encapsulated in the recurring phrase, "And Enoch walked with God." This expression signifies a life of profound piety, unwavering devotion, and intimate communion with the Divine. He is understood to have lived a righteous existence, striving to uphold God's ways amidst an era increasingly marked by moral decline and sin. His unique spiritual journey set him apart, illustrating a continuous commitment to God's will. Genesis concludes his story with the enigmatic declaration, "and he was not, for God took him." Within Jewish tradition, this phrase has elicited various interpretations. Some understand it to signify a unique, divinely orchestrated pious death, where God removed him from the world before his time to prevent him from succumbing to the surrounding wickedness or to reward his exceptional righteousness. Others view it as a spiritual elevation, a removal from earthly existence due to his profound dedication. Regardless of the precise interpretation, Enoch's legacy remains that of a paragon of faith, a man whose life exemplified deep commitment to God, leading to an extraordinary divine intervention in his earthly tenure.

islamic.text: Prophet Nuh (Noah), peace be upon him, is one of the most important prophets in Islam and one of the five messengers of firm resolve (ulu al-'azm), with Ibrahim, Musa, Isa and Muhammad. He is named in 43 verses of the Quran, Surah Nuh (71) is devoted to his mission, and Allah says He chose Adam, Nuh and the families of Ibrahim and Imran above all people of their time (Ali 'Imran 3:33). Islamic tradition, following al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, places him ten generations after Adam, descended through Shith and Idris. He was sent to a people who had turned to idols, venerating images of righteous predecessors — Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq and Nasr (Nuh 71:23). He called them to worship Allah alone for 950 years (Al-'Ankabut 29:14), night and day, openly and in secret, warning them of punishment. They mocked him and refused to leave their idols, and only a few believed, so he called on Allah for help against them. Allah commanded him to build the Ark under His instruction (Hud 11:37), and the leaders of his people mocked him as he built it. He was told to take aboard a pair of every kind, his family except those already condemned, and the believers. Among the disbelievers were his wife and one of his sons, who refused to board and drowned. Water gushed from the earth and poured from the sky, and the Ark sailed through waves like mountains; all who disbelieved perished. Then the earth swallowed its water and the Ark came to rest on Mount Judi (Hud 11:36–48), traditionally identified with a peak in the Cudi range in southeastern Turkey, near the Iraqi border. In Islamic genealogical tradition his three surviving sons, Sam, Ham and Yafith, became the ancestors of the Semitic, Hamitic and Japhetic peoples. The Quran praises him as a grateful servant (Al-Isra 17:3), and tafsir treats the time after the Flood as the second age of humanity.

christian.text: Noah (Nuh in the Islamic tradition), a righteous man blameless among his generation, walked faithfully with God at a time when human wickedness covered the earth. As recorded in Christian scripture, particularly Genesis 6–9, God observed the pervasive corruption and grieved that He had made mankind. Deciding to cleanse the earth with a great flood, God chose Noah and his family to preserve life. He commanded Noah to build a massive ark, providing precise dimensions and instructions for its construction. Noah diligently obeyed, gathering two of every kind of unclean animal and bird, and seven pairs of every clean animal and bird, along with his wife, his three sons—Shem, Ham, and Japheth—and their wives. When Noah was six hundred years old, the rains descended for forty days and forty nights, and the springs of the great deep burst forth, covering the highest mountains. All living creatures outside the ark perished. After 150 days, the waters receded, and the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat. Noah sent out a raven and then doves, one of which returned with a fresh olive leaf, signaling that the land was drying. Upon God's command, Noah and his family emerged, and he built an altar to the Lord, offering sacrifices. God then made a covenant with Noah and all living creatures, promising never again to destroy the earth by flood, setting the rainbow in the sky as an everlasting sign of this promise. From Noah's sons, the earth was repopulated.

jewish.text: Noah (Nuh in the Islamic tradition), born to Lamech, was named Noach, meaning 'comfort,' for he would bring relief from the earth's toil and corruption. Living in a world steeped in extreme violence and moral degradation, Noah uniquely found favor in the eyes of the Lord. The Torah, the foundational scripture of Judaism, describes him as "a righteous man, blameless in his generation," who "walked with God." Witnessing humanity's depravity, God resolved to cleanse the earth with a great flood. Noah alone was chosen to preserve life. He was commanded to build a colossal ark according to divine specifications. He, his wife, his three sons – Shem, Ham, and Japheth – and their wives, along with pairs of all living creatures, entered the ark. When the floodwaters covered the entire earth, all other life perished. After months, the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat. Upon leaving the ark, Noah built an altar and offered sacrifices to God. In response, God established an eternal covenant with Noah and all humanity, promising never again to destroy the world by flood, with the rainbow as its perpetual sign. Noah was also given the Seven Noahide Laws, a universal moral code binding on all mankind. Living 950 years, Noah became a patriarch of renewed civilization, through whom all subsequent generations descended.

bahai.text: Nuh, known as Noah in some traditions, is revered in the Baháʼí Faith as a Manifestation of God, a divinely appointed Messenger in the unbroken chain of Prophets. From Baháʼí sacred texts, particularly the Kitáb-i-Íqán, we understand that Nuh appeared in ancient times, bringing a new Revelation tailored to the spiritual capacity of his generation. His purpose, like all Manifestations, was to educate humanity, uplift souls, and establish a Covenant with God’s people. Nuh's primary mission was to warn his people, who had plunged into heedlessness and idolatry, urging them to turn towards the One True God. Despite his arduous efforts and numerous proofs, the vast majority rejected his divine call, mocking his message and refusing to heed his admonitions. Consequently, Nuh announced the approach of a great deluge. In Baháʼí understanding, this "flood" carried both a literal aspect, confined to a specific region, and a profound spiritual meaning. It symbolized the overwhelming spiritual darkness and corruption that engulfed the disbelievers, separating them from the light of God’s Cause. Those who accepted Nuh’s message and entered the "Ark" were saved. This Ark represents the divine Covenant, the Cause of God, and the teachings of the Manifestation itself. To enter the Ark meant to embrace Nuh’s Cause, attaining spiritual and physical preservation. Through Nuh, God renewed His guidance, ensuring the continuity of divine truth and laying the foundation for future spiritual awakenings.

islamic.text: Prophet Hud, peace be upon him, was a messenger sent by Allah to the ancient Arabian people of 'Ad. The Holy Quran calls him "their brother Hud", one of their own people, showing that prophets come from the communities they are sent to (Al-A'raf 7:65). The eleventh surah, Surah Hud, is named after him, and his story is told in Al-A'raf 7:65–72, Hud 11:50–60, Al-Mu'minun 23:31–41, Ash-Shu'ara 26:123–140, Fussilat 41:15–16 and Al-Ahqaf 46:21–26. Classical sources, including al-Tabari's Tarikh and Ibn Kathir's Qisas al-Anbiya, place 'Ad in al-Ahqaf, the great sand desert of southern Arabia, possibly the Empty Quarter or the Hadramawt region of Yemen. The 'Adites were known for their physical strength, monumental buildings and wealth; the Quran names Iram dhat al-'imad, "Iram of the Pillars", with 'Ad (Al-Fajr 89:6–7). They had turned to the worship of idols, with arrogance and tyranny. Hud said: "O my people! Worship Allah; you have no other god except Him" (Al-A'raf 7:65). He reminded them that their wealth and power came from their Creator, and urged them to repent and seek forgiveness, warning of punishment if they persisted. Their chiefs answered: "We surely see you as a fool, and we certainly think you are a liar" (Al-A'raf 7:66), and they dared him to bring the punishment he warned of. After a prolonged drought, when they saw a cloud approaching their valleys, they said, "This is a cloud bringing us rain"; but it was what they had sought to hasten, a fierce wind carrying a painful punishment (Al-Ahqaf 46:24). Allah sent upon them a furious, bitter wind (rih sarsar 'atiyah) for seven nights and eight days, which destroyed everything, leaving nothing visible but their ruins (Al-Haqqah 69:6–7; Al-Ahqaf 46:25). Allah saved Hud and those who believed with him. Islamic tradition holds his tomb to be at Qabr Hud in the Hadramawt valley of Yemen, a major site of yearly ziyara visits, and counts him as one of the four Arab prophets, with Salih, Shu'ayb and Muhammad.

bahai.text: Húd is honored in the Bahá'í Faith among the Prophets of God whose stories Bahá'u'lláh recounts in the Kitáb-i-Íqán, His foremost doctrinal work. There, Bahá'u'lláh relates that Húd arose after Noah and — for a period which the Íqán, citing the sayings of men, reckons at nearly seven hundred years — patiently exhorted his people to turn towards God. Despite this long and devoted summons, his admonitions bore only increased rebelliousness, and his people persisted in willful blindness. For Bahá'ís, the story of Húd illustrates a recurring pattern in religious history: the Messengers of God are rejected by the very people they are sent to save, yet the divine purpose is never thwarted. His mission stands as a link in the unbroken chain of progressive revelation which, in the Bahá'í view, culminates in this age in Bahá'u'lláh.

islamic.text: Prophet Salih, peace be upon him, was sent by Allah to his own people, the Thamud, a powerful tribe of north-western Arabia (Al-A'raf 7:73). They lived at al-Hijr, "the Stonetown", the name the Quran gives their city, located between Tabuk and Madinah; the site has been called Mada'in Salih, "the cities of Salih", after him since the time of the Prophet Muhammad. Despite Allah's bounties they had turned to idol worship, and Salih called them back to worship Allah alone (7:73). He reminded them that Allah had made them successors after the people of 'Ad, who had been destroyed before them, and that they built palaces on the plains and carved homes into the mountains (7:74). They answered, "O Salih! We truly had high hopes in you before this. How dare you forbid us to worship what our forefathers had worshipped?" (Hud 11:62). Some of the humble believed him, but the arrogant chiefs rejected him (7:75) and demanded a miracle. Allah sent them a she-camel as a sign and a test (7:73; Al-Qamar 54:27): she was to graze freely and not be harmed, and the water was to be shared between her and the tribe, each drinking in turn (54:28). Defying the command, they hamstrung and killed her, and Salih warned them that they had only three more days to enjoy life in their homes (11:65). Surah An-Naml adds that nine men in the city plotted to attack Salih and his family by night (An-Naml 27:48–49). Then an earthquake and a mighty blast seized the Thamud, and they fell lifeless in their homes (7:78; 11:67), while Allah saved Salih and those who believed with him (11:66). Muslim tradition elaborates the story: according to al-Tabari, Salih summoned his people to a mountain where the rock split open to reveal the camel with her young calf; on the days the people could not drink from the water, she gave them milk; after she was killed the calf cried out three times, and the people's faces turned yellow, then red, then black before they died on the third day. Some Islamic scholars hold that Hajar, the mother of Prophet Isma'il, was a granddaughter of Salih.

bahai.text: Ṣáliḥ is honored in the Bahá'í Faith among the Prophets of God whose stories Bahá'u'lláh recounts in the Kitáb-i-Íqán. There, Bahá'u'lláh relates that Ṣáliḥ summoned his people to eternal life and to obedience to God's commandments, exhorting them for more than a century. His people, clinging to the ways of their fathers, rejected his call — answering that their hopes had rested on him until he forbade them to worship what their fathers had worshipped. Their persistent refusal, the Íqán relates, ended in their utter perdition. For Bahá'ís, Ṣáliḥ's story exemplifies the rejection faced by God's Messengers in every age, and forms a link in the chain of progressive revelation which, in the Bahá'í view, culminates in this age in Bahá'u'lláh.

islamic.text: Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham), peace be upon him, is a prophet and messenger of Allah and the ancestor of the Adnanite Arabs and the Israelites. The Holy Quran calls him a model, "devoted to Allah, upright, not a polytheist" (An-Nahl 16:120), and calls Islam millat Ibrahim, the faith of Ibrahim (An-Nahl 16:123). "Allah chose Abraham as a close friend" (An-Nisa 4:125), hence his title Khalilullah. Allah tested him with commands which he fulfilled, and made him a leader for mankind (Al-Baqarah 2:124). From his youth he questioned the idol worship of his people and his father Azar, and by reflecting on the stars, the moon and the sun he declared his devotion to the Lord of all worlds (Al-An'am 6:74–79). Tradition holds that Azar was an idol-sculptor in Ur and that Ibrahim mocked the idols because they could not move or answer. He argued with a king to whom Allah had given kingship: Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west; and the disbeliever was left speechless (Al-Baqarah 2:258). The Quran does not name him; tafsir, including Ibn Kathir's, names him Nimrod. Ibrahim was thrown into a great fire, and Allah said: "O fire, be coolness and safety for Ibrahim" (Al-Anbiya 21:68–69). Tradition adds that Jibril asked if he wished for anything and he replied, "Allah is sufficient for me," and that the fire burned only his chains. Allah showed him how He gives life to the dead through four birds that flew back to him (Al-Baqarah 2:260). He migrated for Allah's sake and prayed for righteous offspring (As-Saffat 37:99–100), and Allah gave him Ismail through Hajar and Ishaq through Sarah. In a dream he saw that he must sacrifice his son, identified in Islamic tradition as Ismail; both submitted, and Allah ransomed the son "with a great sacrifice", a ram according to tradition (As-Saffat 37:102–107). Eid al-Adha commemorates this. Ibrahim and Ismail raised the foundations of the Kaaba (Al-Baqarah 2:125–127), the first house of worship for mankind (Al Imran 3:96), and established the rites of Hajj.
sources: THE-O summary: Abraham in Islam (Wikipedia, en_full) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_in_Islam)

christian.text: According to Christian scripture, Abraham (Ibrahim in the Islamic tradition), a foundational figure in Christian theology, is introduced in Genesis as Abram, called by God from Ur of the Chaldeans. God commanded him to leave his homeland for a land He would show him, making extraordinary promises: to make him a great nation, bless him, make his name great, and through him, bless all families of the earth. This divine call initiated Abraham's profound journey of faith, as he obeyed, trusting in God's unseen plan. Despite his wife Sarah's barrenness and their advanced age, God established a covenant, promising countless descendants and a son, Isaac, through whom the lineage of promise would continue. Abraham's faith reached its zenith when God commanded him to sacrifice Isaac, his only son of promise. Abraham, demonstrating unwavering trust, proceeded with obedience, believing God could even raise the dead. An angel intervened, providing a ram, signifying God's ultimate provision. This narrative, central to the Holy Bible, cemented Abraham's status as the father of faith for both Jews and Christians, lauded in books like Romans and Hebrews. From his descendants came the nation of Israel, and ultimately, Jesus Christ, the fulfillment of the promise that all nations would find blessing through Abraham's seed.

jewish.text: Abraham (Ibrahim in the Islamic tradition), originally Abram, is revered in Jewish tradition as the first patriarch and the father of the Jewish people, his life detailed primarily in Genesis 12–25 within the Torah. Born in Ur Kasdim, his journey of faith began when God commanded him to leave his homeland, promising to make him a great nation, bless him, and through him, bless all families of the earth. Abraham faithfully journeyed to Canaan with his wife, Sarah, then Sarai. God established a covenant with Abraham, promising numerous descendants and Canaan as an everlasting inheritance. As a sign, God commanded circumcision (Brit Milah) for Abraham and his male descendants. Abram's name changed to Abraham, "father of a multitude," and Sarai to Sarah. Despite their advanced age, Sarah bore their son, Isaac, through whom the divine covenant would continue. Abraham faced his ultimate test of faith when God commanded him to sacrifice Isaac on Mount Moriah. Demonstrating unwavering obedience, he prepared to fulfill the command, but an angel intervened, and a ram was offered, solidifying his status as a paragon of faith. Abraham lived a life of devotion, purchasing the Cave of Machpelah for Sarah’s and his own burial, establishing the Jewish claim to the land. His legacy endures as the paradigm of monotheism and the progenitor of the chosen nation.

bahai.text: Ibrahim, known as Abraham, stands revered in the Bahá'í Faith as a mighty Manifestation of God, a divine Messenger who inaugurated a significant spiritual dispensation for humanity. Arising in a world steeped in idolatry, Ibrahim courageously proclaimed the oneness of God, calling all to abandon polytheism and embrace true monotheism. His life exemplified profound detachment from worldly attachments and absolute submission to God's will, most notably in his journey from Ur of the Chaldees and the supreme test of sacrificing his beloved son, an act demonstrating a faith unparalleled in its obedience and love for the Divine. Through him, God established a sacred Covenant, promising future blessings and the continuity of divine guidance, ensuring humanity's spiritual progress. Ibrahim's teachings fostered justice, righteousness, and a deeper understanding of humanity's relationship with its Creator. His Revelation laid foundational spiritual truths, cultivating a fertile ground for the subsequent Manifestations, including Moses, Christ, Muhammad, and ultimately the Báb and Bahá’u’lláh. The sacred Bahá’í writings, particularly Bahá’u’lláh's Kitáb-i-Íqán, elucidate Ibrahim's sublime station and the enduring significance of his mission, affirming his pivotal role in the continuous unfolding of God's ever-advancing civilization for humankind.

islamic.text: Prophet Lut (Lot), peace be upon him, the nephew of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham), was chosen by Allah as a messenger to the people of Sodom and the surrounding cities of the plain. He migrated with Ibrahim, and his story is told in at least fourteen surahs, most fully in Al-A'raf (7:80–84), Hud (11:77–83), Al-Hijr (15:57–77), Ash-Shu'ara (26:160–175), An-Naml (27:54–58) and Al-'Ankabut (29:28–35). His people approached men with desire, waylaid travellers and practised indecency openly in their gatherings (29:29). Lut called them to fear Allah: "Do you approach males among the worlds and leave what your Lord has created for you as mates?" (26:165–166). They mocked him and threatened to expel him and his family, saying, "They are a people who wish to remain chaste" (7:82), and Lut prayed to Allah to save him and his family from what they did (26:169). The angels who had brought Ibrahim the news of Ishaq's birth then came to Lut's house as guests. The townspeople surrounded the house demanding the guests, and Allah blinded their eyes (Al-Qamar 54:37). The angels revealed who they were and told Lut to travel with his family in the dark of night, none of them looking back, except his wife, who would share the fate of the others (11:81); she had inclined to the wrongdoers and was destroyed with the city. The cities were overturned and rained upon with stones of baked clay (sijjil), and Lut and his believing family were saved. Al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir place the cities near the Dead Sea; the Quran calls their ruins a sign for those who pass by them (As-Saffat 37:137–138) and speaks of "the overturned cities" (al-mu'tafikat) as a lasting lesson. In Al-An'am (6:86) Lut is named with Ismail, al-Yasa' and Yunus among those Allah favoured over the people of their time.

christian.text: According to Christian scripture, Lot (Lut in the Islamic tradition), a figure central to several narratives, primarily in Genesis 13–19, was the nephew of Abraham. He accompanied his uncle from Ur of the Chaldeans, through Haran, and into Canaan. When their increasing flocks and herds caused strife between their herdsmen, Lot chose to separate from Abraham, settling in the fertile plains of the Jordan, near the wicked cities of Sodom and Gomorrah. He eventually resided within Sodom itself. During his time in Sodom, Lot was captured in battle but subsequently rescued by Abraham. Later, two angels, sent by God, visited Lot in Sodom. Lot showed them hospitality, but the depraved men of Sodom surrounded his house, demanding the strangers for sexual abuse. In a desperate act to protect his guests, Lot offered his own virgin daughters to the mob, an incident reflecting both his desperate plight and the city's extreme wickedness. The angels intervened, blinding the men and revealing God's plan to destroy the cities. Lot was urged to flee with his family. As they escaped, Lot’s wife disobediently looked back at the burning cities and was turned into a pillar of salt. Lot and his two daughters found refuge in a cave. Fearing the loss of their lineage, his daughters made their father drunk on two successive nights and conceived sons by him, who became the ancestors of the Moabites and Ammonites. Despite the complexities of his life and choices, 2 Peter 2:7–8 refers to Lot as a "righteous man, who was distressed by the depraved conduct of the lawless." His story serves as a biblical warning against worldliness and highlights God's judgment on sin.

jewish.text: According to the Hebrew Bible, Lot (Lut in the Islamic tradition), the nephew of Abraham, accompanied his uncle on the momentous journey from Ur of the Chaldeans to the land of Canaan. As their flocks and possessions multiplied, conflict arose between their respective herdsmen. To avoid further discord, Abraham generously offered Lot the choice of land. Lot surveyed the fertile Jordan plain and chose to settle near the city of Sodom, though its inhabitants were known for their great wickedness. Lot was later captured during a regional war, prompting Abraham to lead a daring rescue mission. When the Lord determined to destroy Sodom and Gomorrah for their egregious sins, two divine messengers appeared to Lot at the gate of Sodom. Lot, demonstrating profound hospitality, urged them to stay at his home. That night, the men of Sodom surrounded the house, demanding that Lot surrender his guests for abuse. Lot bravely protected the messengers, even offering his daughters to the mob. The messengers then revealed their purpose, striking the Sodomites with blindness and urging Lot, his wife, and two unmarried daughters to flee, warning them not to look back. As they escaped, Lot’s wife disobeyed the command and was transformed into a pillar of salt. Lot and his daughters sought refuge in a cave. Believing themselves to be the last remnants of humanity, the daughters each lay with their father, conceiving Moab and Ben-Ammi, the progenitors of the Moabite and Ammonite nations, as recounted in Genesis 19.

islamic.text: Prophet Ismail (Ishmael), peace be upon him, is a prophet in Islam, the firstborn son of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) and Hajar, and Muslims regard him as a direct ancestor of the Prophet Muhammad. The Quran lists him among the prophets (Al-Baqarah 2:136; Ali 'Imran 3:84; An-Nisa 4:163; Al-An'am 6:84–86), praises his patience and righteousness (Al-Anbiya 21:85; Sad 38:48), and calls him true to his promise, a messenger and a prophet who urged his people to pray and give alms (Maryam 19:54–55). By Allah's command, Ibrahim brought Hajar and the infant Ismail to a barren valley that became Makkah (Mecca). Searching for water, Hajar ran seven times between the hills of al-Safa and al-Marwa, which pilgrims re-enact during the Hajj, and water sprang from the ground: the well of Zamzam. The tribe of Jurhum, seeing birds circling over the water, settled there with Hajar's permission, and Ismail grew up among them. Ibrahim's prayer for them is recorded: "Our Lord! I have settled some of my offspring in a barren valley, near Your Sacred House" (Ibrahim 14:37). The Quran tells how Ibrahim raised the foundations of the House, the Kaaba, with Ismail (Al-Baqarah 2:125–127); tradition holds that Ismail was left in charge of its care, though accounts differ on the details. The Quran tells of Ibrahim's dream that he must sacrifice his son, and of the son's reply: "O my dear father! Do as you are commanded. Allah willing, you will find me steadfast." Allah then ransomed him with a great sacrifice, which tradition identifies as a ram (As-Saffat 37:99–113). The Quran does not name the son, but Muslims generally hold that he was Ismail, and the event is remembered each year at Eid al-Adha. According to tradition, Ismail married a woman of Jurhum and, on his father's advice, divorced her and married a second woman of the same tribe. The Arab genealogies trace Adnan, the Quraysh and the Prophet Muhammad back to him through his son Qaydar (Kedar), and Islamic tradition places his death in Makkah.

christian.text: According to Christian scripture, Ishmael (Ismail in the Islamic tradition), whose name means "God hears," is a significant figure primarily detailed in Genesis 16–25. He was the firstborn son of Abraham, conceived with Hagar, Sarah's Egyptian servant, at Sarah's request when she was barren. Before his birth, an angel of the Lord appeared to Hagar in the wilderness, promising her a son and foretelling his character: "He will be a wild donkey of a man; his hand will be against everyone and everyone's hand against him, and he will live in hostility toward all his brothers". The angel also promised that her descendants would be too numerous to count. Ishmael was born when Abraham was eighty-six years old. He was circumcised at the age of thirteen as part of God's covenant with Abraham, along with Abraham and every male in his household. Years later, after Isaac's birth, Sarah saw Ishmael mocking Isaac. This led her to demand that Abraham send Hagar and Ishmael away. Though distressed, Abraham complied after God assured him that He would also make a nation of Ishmael because he was Abraham's offspring. God heard the boy's cry in the wilderness of Beersheba, saving them from perishing by revealing a well of water. Ishmael grew up in the wilderness of Paran, becoming an expert archer, and his mother found him a wife from Egypt. Genesis 25 records twelve sons, who became tribal chiefs, fulfilling God's promise to make a great nation of him. He was present with Isaac at Abraham's burial.

jewish.text: According to the Hebrew Bible, Ishmael (Ismail in the Islamic tradition), whose name means "God hears," holds a significant place primarily in Genesis 16–25. He was the firstborn son of Abraham, born when Abraham was 86 years old, to Sarah's Egyptian handmaid, Hagar. Before his birth, an angel of the Lord appeared to Hagar, prophesying Ishmael's nature as a "wild ass of a man" and promising that his descendants would be too numerous to count. After the miraculous birth of Isaac to Sarah, tensions rose, and Sarah, observing Ishmael mocking, demanded that Abraham cast out Hagar and her son. Abraham was deeply distressed by this request, but God commanded him to heed Sarah, reaffirming His promise that Ishmael would also become a great nation because he was Abraham’s seed. Hagar and Ishmael were sent into the wilderness of Beer-sheba. When their provisions were exhausted and Ishmael lay near death, God heard the boy's cries. An angel called to Hagar, revealing a well that saved their lives. God remained with Ishmael as he grew, dwelling in the wilderness of Paran, becoming a skilled archer. His mother arranged his marriage to a woman from Egypt. Ishmael had twelve sons who became tribal chiefs, progenitors of twelve nations, fulfilling God's promise of a great lineage. He lived to be 137 years old, and ultimately joined his half-brother Isaac in burying their father Abraham.

islamic.text: Prophet Ishaq (Isaac), peace be upon him, is a prophet and patriarch in Islam, the second son of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) by his wife Sarah, and the younger half-brother of Ismail (Ishmael). He is named in seventeen verses of the Quran and is consistently praised as righteous, a prophet and a recipient of divine guidance. His birth was a glad tiding from Allah. The Quran tells how angels came to Ibrahim and Sarah as guests and announced that the aged couple would have a son, and Sarah, long past childbearing age, laughed at the news (Hud 11:69–73; Adh-Dhariyat 51:24–30). Surah As-Saffat records: "We gave him good news of Ishaq — a prophet, and one of the righteous. We blessed him and Ishaq as well" (37:112–113). Muslim scholars of the classical period disagreed over which of Ibrahim's sons was the one offered in sacrifice (the dhabih). Al-Tabari preserved both views, but from Ibn Kathir onward the dominant Sunni position has been that it was Ismail, with Ishaq's birth promised only after that test was complete; the order of Surah As-Saffat, where the promise of Ishaq follows the sacrifice story, is read as supporting this. The Quran names Ishaq with Ibrahim and Ya'qub (Jacob) among Allah's chosen servants, "men of strength and insight" (Sad 38:45–47). He is the father of Prophet Ya'qub, through whom the line of prophets of the Children of Israel descended, including Yusuf, Musa, Dawud, Sulayman and Isa. Islamic tradition, drawing on Ibn Ishaq, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, places his life in the land of Canaan and gives him a long lifespan.

christian.text: According to Christian scripture, Isaac (Ishaq in the Islamic tradition), whose name means "laughter," is a pivotal patriarch, primarily recounted in Genesis 21–35. Born miraculously to Abraham and Sarah in their old age, his birth fulfilled God's promise that Abraham would be the father of many nations. He was circumcised on the eighth day, a sign of the covenant. One of the most profound events of his life was God's command to Abraham to offer Isaac as a sacrifice on Mount Moriah. Isaac willingly carried the wood for his own sacrifice, a moment seen by Christians as a powerful foreshadowing of Christ's sacrifice. An angel of the Lord intervened, stopping Abraham and providing a ram instead, reaffirming God's promise. Later, Isaac married Rebekah, chosen by Abraham's servant. After twenty years of barrenness, Isaac prayed, and Rebekah conceived twins, Esau and Jacob. God revealed that the older would serve the younger. Isaac, favoring Esau, was later deceived by Rebekah and Jacob into giving the patriarchal blessing to Jacob. He experienced God's presence and reaffirmation of the Abrahamic covenant during his life, particularly during his time in Gerar where God blessed him abundantly despite conflict over wells. Isaac lived to be 180 years old and was buried with his parents in the cave of Machpelah, a testament to God's faithfulness across generations.

jewish.text: Isaac (Ishaq in the Islamic tradition), known in Hebrew as Yitzchak, stands as a pivotal patriarch in Jewish tradition, with his life detailed in Genesis within the sacred Torah. His birth was a divine miracle, promised by God to Abraham, then 100, and Sarah, 90, bringing forth laughter, from which his name derives. Circumcised on the eighth day as commanded, Isaac's unwavering faith and obedience were supremely tested during the Akedah, the Binding. Here, as a young man, he willingly accompanied his father Abraham up Mount Moriah, prepared to be offered as a sacrifice by divine command, only to be spared by an angel of God. This profound event solidified his unique role in the eternal covenant. He later married Rebekah, a kinswoman, and after years of barrenness, they were blessed with twin sons, Jacob and Esau. Isaac was the first of the patriarchs to be born in the Land of Israel and notably, he never departed from it, establishing his household there and redigging wells of his father Abraham. Though he faced famine, God commanded him to remain in the land, promising blessings. In his advanced age, blind, Isaac mistakenly bestowed the primary blessing of the birthright upon Jacob, believing him to be Esau, an event that profoundly shaped the future lineage and destiny of the Jewish people. Isaac, who lived to 180, remains an enduring symbol of devotion and a vital link in the unbroken chain of God’s covenant with Israel, buried ultimately in the Cave of Machpelah alongside his revered parents.

islamic.text: Prophet Yaqub (Jacob), peace be upon him, was the son of Prophet Ishaq (Isaac) and grandson of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham). He is also called Isra'il, and the Children of Israel (Bani Isra'il) descend from him. He is mentioned by name in the Quran sixteen times, and he preached the same pure monotheism as his forefathers. When Ibrahim had left his people and the idols they worshipped, Allah granted him Ishaq and Yaqub, made each of them a prophet, and blessed them with honourable mention (Maryam 19:49–50). Allah also made them leaders guiding by His command and inspired them to do good deeds, establish prayer and pay alms (Al-Anbiya 21:72–73); the Quran calls Ibrahim, Ishaq and Yaqub men of strength and insight, among the chosen and the finest (Sad 38:45–47). Yaqub had twelve sons, among them Prophet Yusuf (Joseph). When the young Yusuf told him of his dream of eleven stars, the sun and the moon prostrating to him, Yaqub understood its meaning and warned him not to tell his jealous brothers (Yusuf 12:4–6). He feared that a wolf might devour the boy, but the brothers took Yusuf and threw him into a well, then brought back his shirt stained with false blood; Yaqub did not believe them and resolved on "beautiful patience" (12:13–18). Years later he reluctantly let his youngest son Binyamin (Benjamin) go to Egypt (12:63–66), and when the brothers returned without him he again put his trust in Allah (12:83). His eyes turned white from grief for Yusuf, yet he said he complained of his sorrow only to Allah, and he sent his sons to search for Yusuf, telling them never to lose hope in Allah's mercy (12:84–87). When Yusuf's shirt was cast over his face he regained his sight (12:93–96); he promised to pray for his sons' forgiveness (12:98), and Allah reunited the family in Egypt, where they bowed before Yusuf (12:100). Ibrahim had taught this faith to his sons, and Yaqub gave his own sons the same final counsel: to worship the One God and not to die except as Muslims, in full submission to Allah (Al-Baqarah 2:132–133).

christian.text: According to Christian scripture, Jacob (Yaqub in the Islamic tradition), a pivotal patriarch in the Christian faith, was the son of Isaac and Rebekah, and the younger twin brother of Esau. His extensive life story is primarily chronicled in Genesis within the Holy Bible. Jacob famously acquired his elder brother Esau’s birthright for a modest meal and, with his mother Rebekah’s assistance, deceitfully obtained the patriarchal blessing intended for Esau from their blind father, Isaac. Fleeing Esau’s anger, Jacob journeyed to Haran. During his travels, he encountered a divine vision at Bethel, known as Jacob's Ladder, where God reiterated the covenant first made with Abraham and Isaac. In Haran, Jacob labored for his uncle Laban, marrying Leah and Rachel, and fathering twelve sons who would become the progenitors of the twelve tribes of Israel, along with a daughter. Upon his return to Canaan, Jacob wrestled with a mysterious figure, often understood as an angel or God, at Peniel, resulting in his name being changed to Israel, meaning "he struggles with God." He subsequently reconciled with Esau. Later in life, during a severe famine, Jacob moved his family to Egypt, where he was reunited with his long-lost son Joseph. Jacob died in Egypt but, according to his wishes and God's promise, his body was carried back to Canaan for burial in the Cave of Machpelah with his ancestors.

jewish.text: Jacob (Yaqub in the Islamic tradition), known in Hebrew as Yaakov, a revered patriarch of the Jewish people, was the son of Isaac and Rebekah, and grandson of Abraham, as recounted in the sacred text of Genesis. Born grasping the heel of his twin brother Esau, he later acquired Esau's birthright and received his father's blessing through his mother’s guidance. Fleeing Esau’s wrath, Jacob journeyed to Haran, where he famously dreamt of a ladder reaching to heaven, with angels ascending and descending, and God promising him the land and numerous descendants. In Haran, he served Laban, marrying Leah and Rachel, and fathered twelve sons—the progenitors of the twelve tribes of Israel—and a daughter, Dinah. Returning to Canaan, Jacob wrestled with a divine being at the Jabbok ford, sustaining a hip injury. It was there he was renamed Israel (Yisrael), meaning "he who struggles with God," because he had striven with God and men and prevailed. He reconciled with Esau and settled in the land. Jacob’s deep affection for his son Joseph led to family discord, culminating in Joseph’s sale into slavery. Years later, during a famine, Jacob and his entire household descended to Egypt, reuniting with Joseph. Before his death in Egypt, Jacob blessed each of his sons. His body was returned to Canaan and interred in the Cave of Machpelah, the ancestral burial ground.

islamic.text: Prophet Yusuf (Joseph), peace be upon him, was the son of Prophet Yaqub, son of Ishaq, son of Ibrahim. His story is told in full in Surah Yusuf, the twelfth chapter of the Quran, which calls it "the best of stories" (Yusuf 12:3). As a boy he dreamed that eleven stars, the sun and the moon prostrated to him (12:4); his father understood the dream and told him not to relate it to his brothers (12:5). Resenting him, the brothers threw him into the bottom of a well (12:15) and brought their father his shirt stained with false blood, claiming a wolf had eaten him, which Yaqub did not believe (12:18). A passing caravan found Yusuf and sold him in Egypt to al-'Aziz, a high official (12:21). When Yusuf grew to manhood, the official's wife tried to seduce him; he refused, and his shirt, torn from behind, showed that her accusation was false (12:28). He chose prison over sin (12:33). In prison he interpreted the dreams of two fellow prisoners (12:36–41), and both came true. When the king dreamed of seven fat cows eaten by seven lean ones (12:43), Yusuf, still in prison, explained it as seven years of plenty followed by seven of famine and advised storing the grain (12:47). When the king summoned him, he first asked that his name be cleared (12:50); the king then freed and honoured him, and at Yusuf's request put him in charge of the storehouses of the land (12:55). During the famine his brothers came to Egypt and did not recognise him (12:58); he later revealed himself and forgave them (12:90–92). Yaqub, who had lost his sight through grief, regained it through Yusuf's shirt (12:93, 12:96), and the family moved to Egypt and prostrated before Yusuf, fulfilling his childhood dream (12:100). He is named in the Quran in Al-An'am 6:84. In a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad named him among the most honourable of people, a prophet who was the son, grandson and great-grandson of prophets.

christian.text: According to Christian scripture, Joseph (Yusuf in the Islamic tradition), a central figure in Genesis 37–50, was the beloved son of Jacob. His father's favoritism, symbolized by a coat of many colors, and prophetic dreams of his family bowing to him, incited his brothers' envy. They conspired against him, ultimately selling him into slavery, and he was brought to Egypt. There, Joseph served in Potiphar's household but was falsely accused by Potiphar's wife and imprisoned. Even in prison, God was with Joseph. He interpreted the dreams of two fellow prisoners, accurately predicting their fates. Later, Pharaoh summoned Joseph to interpret his disturbing dreams of seven fat cows and seven thin cows, and seven full ears of grain and seven withered ears. Joseph revealed these foretold seven years of abundance followed by seven years of severe famine. Impressed by Joseph's wisdom and divine insight, Pharaoh elevated him to second-in-command over all Egypt, entrusting him with preparing for the coming scarcity. When the famine struck, Joseph's management saved Egypt and the surrounding lands. His brothers, driven by hunger, traveled to Egypt seeking food. Joseph recognized them, put them through tests, and eventually revealed his identity, forgiving them for their past wrongs. He brought his entire family, including his father Jacob, to settle in Egypt, where they prospered. Joseph’s life exemplifies God's providential hand, turning evil into good and demonstrating faithfulness through suffering to ultimate exaltation, laying the groundwork for the nation of Israel's growth.

jewish.text: According to the Hebrew Bible, Joseph (Yusuf in the Islamic tradition), son of Jacob and Rachel, was deeply loved by his father, who gifted him a special tunic. His elder brothers, resentful of Jacob's favoritism and Joseph’s prophetic dreams, conspired against him. They cast him into a pit and subsequently sold him into slavery to Midianites, who brought him to Egypt. There, Joseph was purchased by Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh. Despite serving faithfully, he was falsely accused by Potiphar's wife and imprisoned. In prison, Joseph's ability to interpret dreams became apparent, correctly foretelling the fates of Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker. Years later, Pharaoh, troubled by his own dreams, summoned Joseph. Joseph interpreted them as signifying seven years of abundance followed by seven years of severe famine. Impressed, Pharaoh appointed Joseph as viceroy of Egypt, tasking him with preparing for the impending scarcity. Joseph wisely managed the land, storing grain during the years of plenty. When the famine struck, Joseph's brothers journeyed to Egypt seeking food. Joseph recognized them but concealed his identity, testing their character before finally revealing himself. Overcome with emotion, he forgave his brothers, understanding that God had sent him ahead to preserve their family. Jacob and his entire household then relocated to Egypt, settling in Goshen. Joseph sustained his family throughout the remaining years of famine. He lived to see his grandchildren and, before his death, made his brothers promise to carry his bones from Egypt to the Land of Israel when God would eventually redeem them. His story is extensively recounted in Genesis, part of the Torah.

islamic.text: Prophet Ayyub (Job), peace be upon him, is a prophet of Allah whom the Holy Quran describes as a righteous servant, tested by long suffering, who never lost faith. He is named among those to whom Allah sent revelation (An-Nisa 4:163) and among the guided prophets given prophethood (Al-An'am 6:84). He called to his Lord: "Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful" (Al-Anbiya 21:83), and he cried out that Satan had afflicted him with distress and suffering (Sad 38:41). Allah told him to strike the ground with his foot, and a cool spring gushed forth for washing and drinking; Allah removed his affliction and gave him back his family, twice as many, as a mercy and a lesson (Al-Anbiya 21:84; Sad 38:42–43). Allah told him to take a bundle of grass in his hand and strike with it, and not break his oath, and praised him: "We found him patient, an excellent servant. Indeed, he was one repeatedly turning back to Allah" (Sad 38:44). According to Ibn Kathir, Ayyub had been very rich, with much land, many animals and children, all of which he lost, and he was then struck with a skin disease of sores as a test; he remained steadfast and patient. Ibn Kathir relates that Satan heard the angels praise Ayyub as the most faithful man of his generation and sought to turn him from Allah, and Allah allowed the trial, knowing Ayyub would never turn away. When Satan failed, he turned to Ayyub's wife, who did not lose faith but wept and asked him to pray for relief; Ayyub rebuked her and swore to strike her a hundred times. After he was cured, Allah told him to strike her once with a hundred blades of grass, so he kept his oath without hurting her; preachers cite this as a reminder to be kind to wives. Tradition adds that his wealth was restored. Early commentators traced his lineage to Ibrahim through Esau, son of Ishaq, and tradition places him after Yusuf among the prophets, preaching to his own people. Tradition also holds that in Paradise he will lead those who patiently endured.
sources: THE-O summary: Job in Islam (Wikipedia, en_full) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Job_in_Islam)

christian.text: According to Christian scripture, Job (Ayyub in the Islamic tradition), whose story is recounted in the Book of Job, was a righteous man of the land of Uz, blameless and upright, who feared God and shunned evil. He was greatly blessed with a large family and immense wealth. Satan, challenging God, claimed Job’s piety was conditional on his prosperity. God permitted Satan to test Job, initially allowing him to lose all his possessions and his ten children. Despite these devastating losses, Job worshipped God, declaring, "The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away; may the name of the Lord be praised," and did not sin. Satan was then permitted to afflict Job with painful sores from head to foot. Even his wife urged him to curse God and die, but Job refused, asserting, "Shall we accept good from God, and not trouble?" Three friends came to comfort him, but their counsel soon turned to accusation, insisting Job must have secretly sinned to deserve such suffering.Job, however, maintained his innocence, longing to understand God’s purpose. Finally, God spoke to Job from a whirlwind, revealing His omnipotence and wisdom, to which Job humbly submitted. God then rebuked Job's friends for their incorrect understanding and restored Job’s fortunes, giving him twice what he had before, and granting him a new family and a long life. Job's endurance through undeserved suffering serves as a profound testament to faith and a deep exploration of divine sovereignty in Christian tradition.

jewish.text: According to the Hebrew Bible, Job (Ayyub in the Islamic tradition), a righteous man from the land of Uz, is a central figure in the Ketuvim section of the Tanakh, specifically the Book of Job (Iyov). He was known for his piety, wealth, and large family, leading a blameless life and fearing God. According to the narrative, Satan, the Accuser, challenged God, asserting that Job's righteousness stemmed solely from the blessings he received. God permitted Satan to test Job, stipulating only that his life be spared. Job subsequently endured immense suffering. He lost all his children, his vast livestock, and his health, afflicted by painful boils. Despite his wife urging him to curse God and die, Job steadfastly refused, declaring, "The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord." Three friends came to comfort him but spent weeks debating with Job, suggesting his misfortune was a consequence of hidden sins. Job maintained his innocence, wrestling with the apparent injustice of his suffering but never abandoning his faith. Eventually, God spoke to Job from a whirlwind, revealing His infinite wisdom and omnipotence, prompting Job to humble himself and repent for questioning divine ways. God then restored Job's fortunes twofold, blessed him with new children, and granted him a long, fulfilling life.

islamic.text: Prophet Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was a messenger of Allah sent to the people of Madyan (Midian) (Al-A'raf 7:85), who are also called the Companions of the Wood (Ashab al-Aykah) (Ash-Shu'ara 26:176); one explanation is that the name refers to their worship of a large tree. He is named in the Quran eleven times and is believed to have lived after Ibrahim (Abraham). Muslims count him, with Hud, Salih and Muhammad, among the four Arabian prophets, and Ibn Kathir records that he was known as "the eloquent preacher among the prophets" because, according to tradition, he was granted eloquence in his language. His people worshipped idols, cheated in weights and measures, lay in ambush on the roads and spread corruption in the land (7:85–86). Shu'ayb called them to worship Allah alone, to give full measure and weight and not to defraud people of their goods (7:85; Hud 11:84–85). He warned them that they could suffer what had struck the peoples of Nuh, Hud and Salih, and that the people of Lut were not far from them (11:89). They told him that, were it not for his clan, they would have stoned him; he replied, "Do you have more regard for my clan than for Allah?" (11:91–92). They threatened to expel him and the believers from their land unless they returned to their faith (7:88), and they said he was simply bewitched (26:185). When they refused to repent, Allah destroyed the disbelievers: the Quran speaks of an overwhelming earthquake (7:91), a mighty blast (11:94) and the torment of the day of the cloud (26:189), while Shu'ayb and those who believed with him were saved by a mercy from Allah (11:94). Muslim tradition, from the early commentators onward, almost universally identifies him with the father-in-law of Musa (Moses), though some scholars reject this; Ibn Kathir gives his lineage as Shu'ayb son of Mikil, son of Madyan, son of Ibrahim. One tomb traditionally attributed to him lies in Wadi Shu'ayb in Jordan, west of the town of Mahis.

christian.text: Islamic tradition sometimes identifies Shu'ayb with Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, though many scholars distinguish them. According to Christian scripture, Jethro, a significant figure in the Book of Exodus, was a priest of Midian and Moses' father-in-law. Moses encountered Jethro after fleeing Egypt, having killed an Egyptian. He found refuge in Midian, where he helped Jethro's daughters at a well. Jethro, also identified as Reuel in some scriptures, welcomed Moses into his home and eventually gave him his daughter Zipporah in marriage. For many years, Moses lived in Midian, tending Jethro’s flocks, before his divine encounter at the burning bush. After the miraculous deliverance of the Israelites from Egypt, Jethro heard of the Lord’s powerful deeds. He journeyed to meet Moses in the wilderness at the mountain of God, bringing Moses’ wife Zipporah and their two sons, Gershom and Eliezer. Jethro rejoiced at all the goodness the Lord had shown Israel, offering burnt offerings and sacrifices to God, declaring, "Now I know that the Lord is greater than all gods." Observing Moses laboriously judging the people all day, Jethro offered crucial counsel: to delegate authority by appointing trustworthy men to serve as judges over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens. Moses adopted this wise counsel, establishing a more efficient system of justice. Having imparted his wisdom, Jethro then departed from the Israelite camp and returned to his own land. His story is primarily found in Exodus 2 and 18.

jewish.text: Islamic tradition sometimes identifies Shu'ayb with Jethro (Yitro), though many scholars distinguish them. Jethro, known as Yitro in Hebrew, was the father-in-law of Moses, a righteous gentile, and a priest of Midian according to the Torah. Initially called Reuel, he is believed to have adopted the name Jethro, meaning "his abundance," after embracing the worship of the one God. Rabbinic tradition suggests he was a prominent figure who, through his own intellectual journey, abandoned all forms of idolatry, a decision that led to his ostracization by his own people. Moses, fleeing Egypt, found refuge with Jethro after an encounter at a well where he defended Jethro's daughters. Jethro welcomed Moses into his household, offering him hospitality and eventually his daughter Zipporah in marriage. Jethro provided Moses with a home and support during his years in Midian before Moses received his prophetic calling at the burning bush. Following the Exodus, Jethro journeyed to reunite with Moses and witness the miracles of God. Observing Moses burdened by the immense responsibility of judging the people's disputes, Jethro offered profound counsel, recorded in Exodus 18. He advised Moses to delegate judicial authority, appointing capable men to serve as judges over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens, thereby establishing a structured legal system. This wise counsel was adopted by Moses, proving instrumental in the governance of the nascent Israelite nation. After partaking in offerings to God with the elders of Israel, Jethro returned to his own land, revered for his wisdom and righteous conversion.

islamic.text: Prophet Musa (Moses), peace be upon him, son of Imran and brother of Prophet Harun (Aaron), is one of the most revered prophets and messengers in Islam and the most frequently mentioned person in the Quran, named 136 times, with his life told more fully than that of any other prophet (Ta-Ha 20; Al-Qasas 28). He was born to an Israelite family in Egypt when Pharaoh (Fir'awn) was killing the newborn Israelite boys. At Allah's instruction his mother set him in a basket on the Nile, and he was found by Pharaoh's wife, named Asiya in hadith, who had him adopted. Tradition adds that he refused every wet nurse until his sister brought their mother, who became his nurse. According to an Isra'iliyyat report, as a child he was tested with a plate of rubies and a plate of glowing coals; Jibril guided his hand to a coal, which burned his tongue and left him with a speech defect. As a man he struck and killed an Egyptian who was fighting an Israelite, and repented to Allah; when Pharaoh ordered his death he fled to Midian. There he watered the flocks of two women, and their father, generally held to be Prophet Shu'ayb, gave him a daughter in marriage in return for eight years of work. At the sacred valley of Tuwa near Mount Tur, Allah called him to prophethood and spoke to him directly (An-Nisa 4:164), so he is called Kalim Allah, "the one to whom Allah spoke". Sent to Pharaoh to free the Children of Israel, he showed miracles by Allah's leave: his staff became a serpent and his hand shone with light. After Pharaoh's defiance and the plagues on Egypt (Al-A'raf 7:103–156), Allah parted the Red Sea for Musa and his people, and Pharaoh and his army drowned. On Mount Tur he received the Tawrat on tablets as guidance and light; in his absence his people worshipped the golden calf (Al-Baqarah 2:51), which he condemned on his return. One of the ulu al-'azm, the messengers of firm resolve, he led his people through the wilderness and, in Islamic tradition, died within sight of the Promised Land. Hadith reports say he met the Prophet Muhammad in the heavens on the Night Journey (Isra' and Mi'raj) and urged him to ask for fewer daily prayers, until fifty became five. Muslims see his life as a spiritual parallel to that of the Prophet Muhammad, likening the Exodus from Egypt to the Hijra from Makkah to Medina, both made in the face of persecution.

christian.text: Moses (Musa in the Islamic tradition), a foundational figure in Christian scripture, was born in Egypt while Pharaoh ordered the killing of Israelite male infants. Saved by his mother, he was found in a basket on the Nile and raised in Pharaoh's household. After killing an Egyptian, Moses fled to Midian, where God appeared to him in a burning bush, revealing Himself as "I Am" and commissioning him to deliver the Israelites from slavery. Empowered by God, Moses returned to Egypt, confronting Pharaoh and unleashing ten devastating plagues, culminating in the Passover. This led to the miraculous Exodus – the liberation of the Israelites, who then passed through the parted Red Sea, escaping Pharaoh's army. In the wilderness, on Mount Sinai, God gave Moses the Ten Commandments and the entire Law, establishing a covenant with Israel. Moses faithfully guided the people for forty years, witnessing God's provision. Due to a single act of disobedience, he was permitted only to view the Promised Land from Mount Nebo before his death, having completed his divine mission as recorded in Exodus through Deuteronomy within the Holy Bible.

jewish.text: Moses (Musa in the Islamic tradition), or Moshe Rabbeinu (Our Teacher Moses), is the most revered prophet in Jewish tradition, through whom the entire Torah was given. Born during the brutal enslavement of the Israelites in Egypt, he was hidden by his mother, Yocheved, and placed in a basket on the Nile, where Pharaoh's daughter discovered and raised him. As an adult, he fled Egypt after killing an abusive taskmaster, finding refuge in Midian, where he married Zipporah. At Mount Horeb (Sinai), God appeared to Moses in a burning bush, commissioning him to lead the Israelites out of bondage. Returning to Egypt, Moses, aided by his brother Aaron, confronted Pharaoh, bringing the Ten Plagues upon Egypt until Pharaoh released the people. Moses then led the Exodus, miraculously parting the Red Sea for the Israelites to cross. At Mount Sinai, he ascended to receive the Divine Law, encompassing the Ten Commandments and all subsequent mitzvot, directly from God. For forty years, Moses guided the Israelites through the wilderness, building the Mishkan (Tabernacle) as a dwelling for God's presence, and preparing them for entry into the Land of Israel. Though he led them to the very border, he was not permitted to enter the land himself due to an earlier transgression. Before his passing at the age of 120 on Mount Nebo, God showed him the Promised Land, and he designated Joshua as his successor. Moses remains the unparalleled prophet, the conduit for God's eternal covenant with the Jewish people.

bahai.text: Musa, known as Moses, stands as one of the most revered Manifestations of God, shining brightly in the sacred lineage of divine educators. Baháʼí teachings affirm His exalted station as a Bearer of a new Revelation, specifically commissioned by God to guide humanity and foster the spiritual maturity of humankind. His monumental mission was to deliver the children of Israel from the cruel bondage of Pharaoh in Egypt, leading them towards freedom and spiritual renewal. On Mount Sinai, Musa communed with God, receiving the divine Law, famously including the Ten Commandments, which formed the bedrock of a sacred covenant with His people. The Torah stands as the Holy Book revealed through Him, containing His laws and guidance for that specific era. The Dispensation of Musa, while perfect and essential for its time, was a vital stage in the progressive unfolding of God's plan for humanity. His laws, though strict and necessary for the spiritual development of a nascent people, were preparatory, designed to educate and refine. Baháʼu'lláh explains that each Manifestation builds upon the last, perfecting and adapting the divine teachings to the needs of an evolving humanity. Musa's profound impact laid the foundation for future Revelations, paving the way for the coming of Christ, Muhammad, and ultimately, the Báb and Baháʼu'lláh, all part of the same eternal truth, fulfilling God's ancient promises. His life exemplifies divine power and unwavering commitment to God's will.

islamic.text: Prophet Harun (Aaron) ibn Imran, peace be upon him, is honoured in Islam as a prophet and messenger of Allah and the elder brother of Prophet Musa (Moses), peace be upon him. Islamic tradition names his father as Imran and his mother as Yukabid, and Maryam (Miriam) was their sister. When Allah sent Musa to Pharaoh, Musa prayed for a helper from his own family and asked that his brother Harun share in his mission, and his prayer was granted (Ta-Ha 20:29–36). Musa described Harun as more eloquent than himself and asked that he be sent with him as a supporter (Al-Qasas 28:34), and Allah says He granted Musa his brother Harun as a prophet out of His mercy (Maryam 19:53). The two brothers were sent together with Allah's signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs (Yunus 10:75), and endured his tyranny and disbelief. After Allah saved them from Pharaoh and his army, Musa went up Mount Tur to receive the Tawrat. He went to meet his Lord for forty nights and left Harun in his place among the Children of Israel (Al-A'raf 7:142). During that time the Samiri led the people into worshipping a calf. Harun warned them that they were being tested by it and urged them to follow him, but they refused to stop until Musa returned (Ta-Ha 20:85–91). When Musa returned and seized him by the head, Harun, calling him "son of my mother", explained that the people had overpowered him and nearly killed him, and that he had feared being blamed for dividing the Children of Israel (Al-A'raf 7:150; Ta-Ha 20:94). Musa then prayed: "My Lord, forgive me and my brother, and admit us into Your mercy" (Al-A'raf 7:151). The Quran sends peace upon Musa and Harun together (As-Saffat 37:120), and in Al-Baqarah 2:248 it speaks of the Ark holding relics of the family of Musa and the family of Harun. In the hadith of the Night Journey, the Prophet Muhammad is reported to have met Harun in the fifth heaven. One Islamic tradition places his tomb on Jabal Harun near Petra, in present-day Jordan.

christian.text: According to Christian scripture, Aaron (Harun in the Islamic tradition), a foundational figure of the Old Testament, was the elder brother of Moses, born to Amram and Jochebed of the tribe of Levi. Chosen by God, he served as Moses’ eloquent spokesman, enabling his brother to confront Pharaoh and lead the Israelites out of bondage in Egypt. Together, as chronicled in Exodus, they performed mighty signs and wonders, including Aaron’s staff transforming into a serpent and its role in the plagues that afflicted Egypt, culminating in the miraculous parting of the Red Sea. He ascended Mount Sinai with Moses, witnessing the giving of the Law. However, during Moses' prolonged absence, Aaron yielded to the people's pressure and fashioned a golden calf for them to worship, an act of idolatry that brought divine displeasure. Despite this lapse, God later consecrated Aaron and his sons as Israel's first priests, establishing the enduring Aaronic priesthood for ministering in the Tabernacle. His divine appointment was further affirmed when his staff miraculously budded and bore almonds, as recorded in Numbers 17. Aaron faithfully served as High Priest until his death at 123 years old on Mount Hor, where his priestly garments were transferred to his son, Eleazar, fulfilling God's sacred ordinances. His life encapsulates themes of divine calling, human weakness, and God's enduring covenant grace.

jewish.text: According to the Hebrew Bible, Aaron (Harun in the Islamic tradition), elder brother of Moses, was born to Amram and Jochebed of the tribe of Levi in Egypt, a narrative central to the Torah. Divinely appointed as Moses' spokesman, he bravely confronted Pharaoh, assisting his brother in demanding the Israelites' release and performing the ten plagues that ultimately led to the liberation from bondage. Following the miraculous crossing of the Red Sea and at Mount Sinai, Aaron was consecrated by Moses as the first High Priest, the Kohen Gadol, an office he held for forty years in the wilderness. His sacred duties involved ministering in the Tabernacle, offering sacrifices, and providing spiritual guidance to the nascent nation. This divine calling was confirmed when his staff miraculously blossomed, affirming his and his descendants' eternal priesthood, the Kohanim. Though he regrettably succumbed to the people's demands during the sin of the Golden Calf, later tradition emphasizes his remorse and God's ultimate forgiveness. Aaron was widely revered for his character, exemplified by his profound love of peace and his tireless pursuit of reconciliation among the Israelites, a virtue deeply cherished in Jewish teachings. He passed away on Mount Hor at the age of 123, a consequence of his and Moses' actions at the Waters of Meribah. His enduring legacy as the patriarch of the priesthood and a symbol of peace continues to inspire.

islamic.text: Prophet Dhul-Kifl, peace be upon him, is a prophet of Allah named twice in the Holy Quran, each time in a list of prophets. In Surah Al-Anbiya, Allah says: "And remember Ishmael, Enoch and Dhul-Kifl. They were all steadfast. We admitted them into Our mercy, for they were truly of the righteous" (Al-Anbiya 21:85–86), counting him "of the patient" (min al-sabirin) with Ismail and Idris. In Surah Sad he is named with Ismail and Al-Yasa: "All are among the best" (min al-akhyar) (Sad 38:48). The Quran does not detail the events of his life, his mission or the people he was sent to, and his identity is not known for certain. His name means "possessor of the kifl", the same pattern as Dhul-Qarnayn and Dhun-Nun, "the One with the Fish", a title of Prophet Yunus. Kifl is an old Arabic word meaning "double" or "duplicate", so the name is usually understood as "possessor of the portion" or "one of a double portion"; it is also explained in Islamic tradition as "the one who took responsibility". Classical commentators such as Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Kathir describe him as a prophetic, saintly man who remained faithful in daily prayer (salah) and worship ('ibada), and he is believed to have been raised by Allah to a high station. Commentators differ on who he was. He has most commonly been identified with the prophet Ezekiel (Hazqiyal in Arabic), and some scholars have suggested the name is a title of Prophet Ayyub (Job), "the man who received recompense twice over", since his family was returned to him. In his Quran commentary, Abdullah Yusuf Ali favoured the Ezekiel identification, noting the shrine at the town of al-Kifl, between Najaf and Hilla in Iraq. That shrine is known by names such as Qabr al-Nabi Dhul-Kifl; according to the Iraqi authorities, in 1316 the Ilkhan Öljaitü took over its guardianship and added a mosque and a minaret. Some also believe a tomb on the hill of Makam Dağı near Ergani, in Diyarbakır, Turkey, is his resting place.

christian.text: Islamic tradition often identifies Dhul-Kifl with the biblical prophet Ezekiel, though this is not certain; the following is Ezekiel's story. Ezekiel, whose name means "God strengthens," was a significant prophet and priest in ancient Israel, son of Buzi. His ministry began around 593 BC, during the Babylonian exile, a pivotal period in Israelite history. God called him to prophecy while he was among the Jewish exiles by the Chebar Canal in Babylon, specifically in the fifth year of King Jehoiachin’s captivity. His divinely appointed mission, as recorded in the Book of Ezekiel in the Christian Old Testament, was primarily to his fellow Jewish captives. Ezekiel's prophecies encompassed several critical themes. He delivered stark warnings of Jerusalem's impending destruction, emphasizing the consequences of Israel's idolatry and rebellion against God. He often performed dramatic symbolic acts, such as lying on his side for days, shaving his head and beard, and eating a meager diet, to powerfully illustrate God's coming judgment. Beyond messages of doom, Ezekiel also brought profound messages of hope and future restoration for the scattered people of Israel, including the famous vision of the valley of dry bones, symbolizing God's power to revive a spiritually dead nation. He also prophesied about the judgment of surrounding nations and envisioned a future, glorious new temple and a restored land, culminating in the promise that "the Lord is there." His detailed and often dramatic visions profoundly shaped the understanding of divine judgment and ultimate redemption within the Christian tradition.

jewish.text: Islamic tradition often identifies Dhul-Kifl with the biblical prophet Ezekiel, though this is not certain; the following is Ezekiel's story. Ezekiel, son of Buzi and a member of the priestly lineage (Kohen), emerged as a pivotal prophet during the Babylonian exile. He was among the Jewish elite deported from Judah to Babylonia in 597 BCE alongside King Jehoiachin, settling by the Chebar Canal. Five years into his exile, at the age of thirty, Ezekiel received his initial divine vision, marked by the profound vision of the Merkavah, the Divine Chariot, a central theme in Jewish mystical thought. His extensive prophetic ministry, documented in the Book of Ezekiel within the Nevi'im section of the Tanakh, spanned more than two decades.
