Through a combination of vivid visions and striking symbolic actions, such as lying on his side for extended periods or shaving his head, Ezekiel delivered God's pronouncements. He steadfastly condemned the widespread idolatry and moral corruption prevalent in Judah, foretelling Jerusalem's impending destruction and the eventual ruin of the Temple, events that tragically materialized in 586 BCE. Despite these severe warnings, Ezekiel also conveyed powerful messages of hope and future redemption. His renowned vision of the Valley of Dry Bones vividly symbolized the eventual spiritual and physical rebirth of the Jewish people and the promise of resurrection. He prophesied the future ingathering of the exiles, the restoration of the Davidic dynasty, and provided a detailed vision for a rebuilt Temple in Jerusalem, underscoring God's enduring covenant, the importance of individual accountability, and ultimate sovereignty over Israel.

islamic.text: Prophet Dawud (David), peace be upon him, is honoured in Islam as a prophet and messenger of Allah and a righteous king of the Children of Israel; the Holy Quran mentions him by name sixteen times. As a young man, in the battle led by King Talut, Dawud killed the warrior Jalut (Goliath), and Allah then gave him kingship and wisdom and taught him what He willed (Al-Baqarah 2:251). Allah gave him the scripture called the Zabur, identified with the Psalms (An-Nisa 4:163; Al-Isra 17:55), which he recited with a beautiful voice. The Quran calls him "the man of strength" who constantly turned to Allah (Sad 38:17). Allah commanded the mountains and the birds to echo His praise along with him (Al-Anbiya 21:79; Saba 34:10), made iron mouldable for him and taught him to make coats of mail (Al-Anbiya 21:80; Saba 34:10–11). Allah made him a khalifa, a vicegerent, on earth (Sad 38:26), a title the Quran otherwise gives only to Adam (Al-Baqarah 2:30). Allah gave both Dawud and his son Sulayman (Solomon), also a prophet and king, sound judgment and knowledge (Al-Anbiya 21:78–79), and gave Dawud the ability to distinguish truth from falsehood in judging (Sad 38:20). The Quran also alludes to a test, in his role as judge, after which Dawud sought forgiveness, bowed down in repentance, and was forgiven (Sad 38:24–25). According to a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad said that the prayer and fasting most beloved to Allah were those of Dawud: he slept half the night, prayed for a third of it and slept for a sixth, and he fasted on alternate days.
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari (hadith on Dawud's prayer and fasting, as cited in THE-O summary)

christian.text: According to Christian scripture, David (Dawud in the Islamic tradition), a central figure of the Bible, first appears as a humble shepherd boy from Bethlehem, the youngest son of Jesse. Despite his youth, God chose him, and the prophet Samuel anointed him as the future king of Israel. His faith and courage were famously displayed when, armed only with a sling and stones, he defeated the Philistine giant Goliath, asserting God’s power over human might. David later ascended to the throne, uniting the tribes of Israel and establishing Jerusalem as his capital. Though a man "after God's own heart," David was not without sin. His most grievous offense involved committing adultery with Bathsheba and arranging the death of her husband, Uriah. Confronted by the prophet Nathan, David showed deep remorse and profound repentance, a testament to his sincere devotion to God. His life, chronicled primarily in the books of Samuel, Kings, and Chronicles, illustrates both divine grace and human fallibility. David’s reign was marked by both military success and personal tragedy, yet his Psalms express profound trust and worship. Crucially for Christians, David is revered as a direct ancestor of Jesus Christ, the Messiah, fulfilling ancient prophecies of a king from the house of David who would reign forever. He is remembered as a powerful king, a gifted psalmist, and a repentant sinner whose lineage carried the promise of salvation.
sources: Bible, Books of Samuel, Kings, Chronicles; Psalms

jewish.text: According to the Hebrew Bible, David (Dawud in the Islamic tradition), son of Jesse from the tribe of Judah, emerged from humble beginnings as a shepherd in Bethlehem. Chosen by God, he was secretly anointed by the prophet Samuel to be the future king of Israel, as recorded in the Books of Samuel within the Tanakh. David first gained renown for his unwavering faith and courage, famously defeating the Philistine giant Goliath with a sling and stone, an act that showcased God's hand guiding a young man against overwhelming odds. After serving King Saul, David faced Saul's jealousy and pursuit but steadfastly refused to harm God's anointed king. Upon Saul's death, David was crowned king over all Israel. He conquered Jerusalem, establishing it as the unified capital and the spiritual center, the City of David, bringing the Ark of the Covenant there. Though a man after God’s own heart, David was not without fault; his sin involving Bathsheba and Uriah brought divine rebuke through the prophet Nathan, to which David responded with profound repentance. His deep piety and expressions of praise are immortalized in many Psalms, earning him the title "sweet singer of Israel." David's reign laid the foundation for an eternal dynasty, with God promising that the Messiah would descend from his lineage, ensuring his enduring significance in Jewish tradition.

islamic.text: Prophet Sulayman (Solomon), peace be upon him, was a prophet and king of the Children of Israel and the son of Prophet Dawud (David); when Dawud died, Sulayman succeeded him as prophet-king (An-Naml 27:16). The Quran mentions him judging together with his father in a dispute over a field, a judgement cited for his wisdom (Al-Anbiya 21:78–79); later commentators such as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir told it as the story of sheep that strayed into a vineyard. Allah subjected the wind to him, made a spring of molten copper flow for him, and placed jinn under his command, who built for him (Saba 34:12–13; Al-Anbiya 21:81–82); according to tradition, their work included the Bayt al-Maqdis, a sacred house of worship in Jerusalem. He was taught the speech of birds (27:16), and in the valley of the ants he understood an ant warning its colony to take shelter lest Sulayman and his armies crush them unknowingly, and he thanked Allah (27:18–19). When the hoopoe returned from Saba (Sheba) with news of a powerful queen whose people worshipped the sun (27:22–23), Sulayman sent her a letter calling her to submit to Allah (27:28–31). A mighty jinn, an ifrit, offered to bring her throne before Sulayman rose from his council, but one who had knowledge of the Scripture brought it to him in the blink of an eye (27:38–40). The queen, whom tradition names Bilqis, then submitted to Allah (27:44). He prayed for a kingdom such as no one after him would have, and Allah granted it (Sad 38:35–40). The Quran states that Sulayman never disbelieved; it was the devils who disbelieved and taught people magic (Al-Baqarah 2:102). He died leaning on his staff, and the jinn working for him did not realise he was dead until a creature ate through the staff and he fell, showing that the jinn do not know the unseen (34:14). The Quran also praises him in other passages, including Al-An'am 6:84 and Sad 38:30–31.

christian.text: According to Christian scripture, Solomon (Sulayman in the Islamic tradition), also known as Jedidiah, was the son of King David and Bathsheba, born in Jerusalem. He succeeded his father as king of Israel, inheriting a covenant with God. Early in his reign, when God appeared to him in a dream at Gibeon, Solomon humbly requested an understanding heart to govern his people justly, rather than asking for wealth or long life. God was pleased with his request and granted him unparalleled wisdom, making him the wisest man who ever lived, a gift famously demonstrated in his judgment between two women claiming the same child. Solomon fulfilled his father's dream by building the magnificent First Temple in Jerusalem, a dedicated house for the Lord, a project detailed in the Holy Bible. His reign was characterized by immense peace, prosperity, and a vast empire, and his wisdom became legendary, drawing rulers like the Queen of Sheba who came to witness it firsthand. He is traditionally credited with writing the books of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs, found in the Christian Old Testament. However, despite his extraordinary blessings, Solomon later strayed from God. He married numerous foreign women who led him to worship their idols, turning his heart away from the Lord. This disobedience ultimately incurred God’s displeasure, leading to the prophecy that his kingdom would be divided after his death, a consequence detailed in the Books of 1 and 2 Kings.
sources: Bible, 1-2 Kings; Proverbs; Ecclesiastes; Song of Songs

jewish.text: According to the Hebrew Bible, Solomon (Sulayman in the Islamic tradition), known as Shlomo in Hebrew, was the son of King David and Bathsheba, chosen by God to succeed his father as king over Israel. His life and reign are extensively documented in the Books of Kings and Chronicles within the Tanakh. Early in his kingship, Solomon sought wisdom from God, who granted him an understanding heart to discern justice, famously demonstrated in his judgment between two women claiming the same child. This divine gift established his reputation for unparalleled sagacity and understanding. Solomon presided over a period of great peace and prosperity for the united monarchy of Israel. His most enduring legacy was the construction of the First Temple in Jerusalem, a magnificent edifice dedicated to God, fulfilling a vision initiated by his father David. He also built his own grand palace and numerous fortified cities, expanding Israel's infrastructure and influence across the region. His fame for wisdom and wealth attracted rulers from distant lands, including the Queen of Sheba, who traveled to witness his glory and test his intellect. Despite his initial devotion, Solomon’s later life was marred by disobedience; he accumulated many foreign wives who led him astray to worship their deities. He built altars for idols, provoking God's anger and leading to the divine decree that the kingdom would be torn from his son after his death, leaving only a remnant for the house of David.
sources: Tanakh, Books of Kings and Chronicles

islamic.text: Prophet Ilyas (Elijah), peace be upon him, is a messenger of Allah named in the Quran. He is listed among the prophets in Surah Al-An'am (6:85), and Surah As-Saffat (37:123–132) tells of his mission. In the Muslim account he was sent to the Children of Israel, who had strayed into idolatry and worshipped an idol called Ba'l, to call them back to the worship of Allah alone. He said to his people, "Will you not fear Allah? Do you call upon Ba'l and abandon the Best of Creators — Allah, your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers?" (As-Saffat 37:124–126). Most of his people rejected him, though a few devoted servants of Allah followed him, and the Quran says the deniers will be brought for punishment, except Allah's chosen servants (37:127–128). The passage closes with Allah's favour upon him: an honourable mention among later generations, "Peace be upon Ilyas", and the statement that he was one of Allah's faithful servants, rewarded as the doers of good are rewarded (37:129–132). Al-Tabari gives his name as Ilyas ibn Yasin, and some scholars trace his descent to the prophet Harun (Aaron). Muslim literature, including Ibn Kathir, places his preaching in the time of Ahab and his wife Jezebel. Some early commentators said he was sent to Baalbek in present-day Lebanon, though the Quran does not name the city. According to reports in al-Tabari and al-Tha'labi, when his people returned to idolatry he was taken up to heaven, having chosen his pupil al-Yasa' (Elisha) to succeed him; Ibn Kathir rejected these ascension reports as Isra'iliyyat. Mystical tradition links Ilyas closely with al-Khidr, and a report cited by Ibn Kathir says the two meet every year.

christian.text: According to Christian scripture, Elijah (Ilyas in the Islamic tradition), a prominent prophet of God in ancient Israel, is extensively chronicled primarily in the books of 1 and 2 Kings of the Holy Bible. He ministered during the tumultuous reign of King Ahab and Queen Jezebel, a period marked by widespread idolatry, particularly the worship of Baal. Elijah boldly confronted Ahab, declaring a severe drought as divine judgment for the nation's apostasy. During this famine, God miraculously sustained Elijah, first by ravens, then through a widow in Zarephath whose jar of flour and jug of oil never ran out; he also raised her son from the dead. His most famous act was the dramatic confrontation on Mount Carmel. There, Elijah challenged 450 prophets of Baal to a contest, demonstrating the supremacy of the Lord. When the Baal prophets failed to summon fire, Elijah’s prayer was answered by fire from heaven, consuming his water-soaked sacrifice, revealing God's power and leading the people to repentance. Though he later fled Jezebel’s wrath and felt despair, God met him on Mount Horeb with a "still small voice." Ultimately, Elijah did not experience death but was taken up to heaven in a whirlwind by a chariot of fire, witnessed by his successor Elisha. Christian tradition recognizes Elijah's future role, prophesied to return before the great and dreadful day of the Lord, and he notably appeared with Moses alongside Jesus at the Transfiguration, underscoring his enduring significance.

jewish.text: Elijah (Ilyas in the Islamic tradition), known in Hebrew as Eliyahu, was a towering prophet in ancient Israel during the tumultuous reign of King Ahab and Queen Jezebel in the 9th century BCE. His compelling story is primarily recounted in the books of Melachim (Kings) within the Nevi'im (Prophets) section of the Tanakh. Elijah emerged as a zealous defender of HaShem, the One God of Israel, fiercely opposing the widespread idolatry and the worship of Baal promoted by the royal court. His prophetic mission began with a declaration of a severe drought to Ahab, after which he was miraculously sustained by ravens and later by a widow in Zarephath, whose oil and flour never ran out. He famously resurrected her son. The pinnacle of his public ministry was the dramatic confrontation on Mount Carmel, where he challenged the 450 prophets of Baal to call down fire from heaven. When only Elijah's sacrifice was consumed by divine fire, the people returned to God, and the Baal prophets were apprehended. Despite his triumph, Elijah fled Jezebel’s wrath to Mount Horeb, where he experienced God's presence not in wind, earthquake, or fire, but in a "still small voice." He then anointed Elisha as his successor. His life concluded not with death, but with a supernatural ascension into heaven, carried by a chariot of fire and horses of fire in a whirlwind. Jewish tradition anticipates Elijah's return before the coming of the Messiah to herald redemption and resolve intricate legal questions, making him a perennial figure of hope and a divine messenger.

islamic.text: Prophet Al-Yasa (Elisha), peace be upon him, is a prophet of Allah named twice in the Holy Quran. In Surah Al-An'am, Allah names the prophets He guided, among them Dawud, Sulayman, Ayyub, Yusuf, Musa, Harun, Zakariyya, Yahya, Isa and Ilyas, and then Ismail, Al-Yasa, Yunus and Lut, "favouring each over other people of their time" (Al-An'am 6:84–86). Of this whole group Allah says that He chose them and guided them to a straight path, and that this is His guidance, which He gives to whomever He wills among His servants (Al-An'am 6:87–88). The same passage says these are the ones to whom Allah gave the Scripture, judgment and prophethood, and tells the Prophet Muhammad to follow their guidance (Al-An'am 6:89–90). In Surah Sad, right after Ibrahim, Ishaq and Yaqub are praised as "men of strength and insight" and "among the chosen and the finest" (Sad 38:45–47), Allah says: "Also remember Ishmael, Elisha and Dhul-Kifl. All are among the best" (Sad 38:48). His Arabic name, Al-Yasa (Alyasa), is the same name that appears in English as Elisha. The Quran does not detail the events of his life. In Islamic tradition, Al-Yasa is widely regarded as the successor of Prophet Ilyas (Elijah), peace be upon him, who is named in the verse just before him in Surah Al-An'am (6:85). Tradition holds that after Ilyas's departure, Al-Yasa carried on the mission of prophethood among the Children of Israel, calling his people away from polytheism and idol worship, back to the worship of Allah alone and obedience to His commands.

christian.text: According to Christian scripture, Elisha (Al-Yasa in the Islamic tradition), a prominent prophet in the ancient history of Israel, is extensively chronicled primarily within the books of 1 and 2 Kings. His divine calling began while he was plowing, when the prophet Elijah cast his cloak upon him, signifying his anointing as Elijah's successor. Elisha then left his fields to serve Elijah, becoming his attendant. Upon Elijah's miraculous ascension to heaven in a whirlwind, Elisha requested and received a double portion of Elijah's spirit, as evidenced by his subsequent powerful ministry. He immediately demonstrated this anointing by parting the Jordan River with Elijah's fallen cloak. Throughout his prophetic career, Elisha performed numerous miracles, testifying to God's power. These included healing the poisonous waters of Jericho, miraculously providing oil for a destitute widow, raising the Shunammite woman's son from the dead, and healing Naaman, a Syrian commander, of leprosy. He also famously made an axe head float and revealed the Syrian king's plans to the king of Israel, demonstrating his supernatural insight and protection over God's people. Elisha served as a spiritual guide and counselor to kings and common people, often intervening in military conflicts and daily life with divine wisdom and power. Even after his death and burial, God’s power was demonstrated when a dead man was restored to life upon touching Elisha's bones, affirming his enduring prophetic legacy in the Christian tradition.

jewish.text: Elisha (also known as Al-Yasa in the Islamic tradition), a pivotal prophet in ancient Israel, is extensively detailed in the Books of Kings within the Tanakh. Called by the prophet Elijah, Elisha, originally a farmer, was chosen by divine instruction to succeed Elijah. He faithfully served his master, witnessing Elijah's miraculous ascent to heaven and receiving a "double portion" of his spirit, an anointing that empowered his own prophetic work. Elisha’s ministry was marked by numerous miracles, demonstrating God's power and direct intervention. He immediately parted the Jordan River with Elijah's mantle, echoing his master’s feat. Among his many wonders, Elisha purified the poisoned waters of Jericho, provided oil for a destitute widow to save her sons, and, most famously, restored the life of the Shunammite woman's son. He also healed Naaman, the Syrian commander, of his leprosy. Throughout his service, his divine insight frequently thwarted the plots of Israel’s enemies. Even after his passing, his sanctity was affirmed; a dead man revived upon touching Elisha's bones, a powerful testament to his enduring spiritual legacy within Jewish tradition.

islamic.text: Prophet Yunus, peace be upon him, known in Islam as Yunus ibn Matta, was a messenger of Allah (An-Nisa 4:163; Al-An'am 6:86). The tenth surah of the Quran, Surah Yunus, is named after him, and he is also called Dhu al-Nun, "the one of the fish" (Al-Anbiya 21:87; Al-Qalam 68:48). Muslim tradition holds that he was from the tribe of Binyamin (Benjamin). He was sent to a large community, often identified as the people of Nineveh, but they rejected his message. Despairing of them, Yunus left his people in frustration without waiting for Allah's permission and fled to a laden ship (As-Saffat 37:140). Lots were drawn, they fell against him, and the fish (al-hut) swallowed him (37:141–142). In the darkness he repented and called out: "There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers", and Allah heard his plea (21:87–88). Had he not glorified Allah, he would have remained inside the fish until the Day of Resurrection (37:143–144). Allah cast him onto the open shore, worn out and ill, and caused a gourd plant to grow over him (37:145–146). He was sent to a hundred thousand or more, and they believed: his people had repented, the punishment was lifted from them, and Allah let them enjoy life for a while (Yunus 10:98; 37:147–148). Al-Tabari records that none of his bones or limbs was injured inside the fish, that Allah made the fish's body transparent so he could see the wonders of the deep, and that he heard the fish praising Allah. According to the accounts of the Prophet Muhammad's life, when Addas, a servant from Nineveh, brought him grapes after he was driven from Ta'if, he called it the town of the righteous Yunus son of Matta and said, "We are brothers. Yunus was a Prophet of God and I, too, am a Prophet of God." In Sahih al-Bukhari he said, "One should not say that I am better than Yunus." A shrine on the hill of Nabi Yunus at Nineveh was long revered as his tomb.

christian.text: According to Christian scripture, Jonah (Yunus in the Islamic tradition), a prophet in ancient Israel, is prominently featured in the book bearing his name. Called by God to preach repentance to the wicked city of Nineveh, Jonah initially disobeyed, choosing instead to flee by ship towards Tarshish. A great storm arose, and believing Jonah to be the cause, the sailors reluctantly cast him overboard. The Lord then appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah, where he remained for three days and three nights. From within the fish's belly, Jonah prayed to God, expressing repentance and faith. Consequently, the fish vomited him onto dry land. God reiterated His command, and Jonah journeyed to Nineveh, proclaiming its impending destruction. To Jonah's surprise and displeasure, the people of Nineveh, from the king to the common person, repented in sackcloth and ashes. Seeing their genuine remorse, God relented from the judgment He had threatened. Jonah, angered by God's mercy towards Nineveh, withdrew. God then used a plant, a worm, and the scorching sun to teach Jonah a profound lesson about compassion and His boundless mercy, extending even to those outside Israel. Jesus Himself referenced Jonah’s three days and three nights in the fish as a prefigurement of His own resurrection, and Nineveh's repentance as a judgment against those who refused to believe in Him, as recorded in the Gospels.

jewish.text: The prophet Jonah (Yonah ben Amittai; Yunus in the Islamic tradition), whose narrative is recounted in the biblical Book of Jonah, was a figure of great significance in Jewish tradition. Commissioned by God to deliver a prophecy of destruction to the wicked city of Nineveh, Jonah initially resisted, attempting to flee God's presence by sailing to Tarshish. A great storm ensued, leading the sailors to cast Jonah into the turbulent waters as the cause of their misfortune. God then appointed a "dag gadol" (great fish) to swallow Jonah, where he remained for three days and three nights, praying fervently from within its belly. Upon Jonah's repentance, the fish vomited him onto dry land. Once more, God instructed Jonah to go to Nineveh. This time, he obeyed, proclaiming the city's impending doom. To Jonah's surprise and dismay, the king and all the people of Nineveh responded with sincere repentance, fasting and turning from their evil ways. Witnessing their genuine change, God relented and spared the city. Jonah, distraught by God's compassion for Nineveh, expressed his unhappiness. God then used a rapid-growing plant, and subsequently a worm and a scorching wind, to teach a profound lesson about divine mercy and the vastness of God's compassion for all creation, including those outside of Israel. His story serves as a central text for reflection on Yom Kippur.

islamic.text: Prophet Zakariya, peace be upon him, is a prophet in Islam and the father of Prophet Yahya (John); his story opens Surah Maryam and is also told in Surah Ali 'Imran. Tradition holds that he was a priest descended from Prophet Dawud (David). Allah entrusted Maryam, mother of Isa (Jesus), to his care, and whenever he visited her in the sanctuary (mihrab) he found her supplied with provisions, at which he marvelled (Ali 'Imran 3:37). Zakariya and his wife were advanced in age and childless, and he was concerned for the continuation of his prophetic line. Fearing for his relatives after him, since his wife was barren, he earnestly prayed to Allah for a righteous heir who would inherit from him and from the family of Ya'qub (Jacob) (3:38; Maryam 19:5–6). Allah answered his prayer (Al-Anbiya 21:89–90). While he stood praying in the mihrab, the angels gave him glad tidings of a son named Yahya, who would confirm a word from Allah and be a prophet (3:39). Astonished, Zakariya asked for a sign to confirm this extraordinary news, and his sign was that he would not speak to people for three days and nights except by gestures, though he was otherwise healthy (3:41; 19:10). He came out from the sanctuary to his people and signalled to them to glorify Allah morning and evening (19:11). In due time his wife conceived and Yahya was born, a blessed child to whom Allah granted wisdom while still young (19:12). Zakariya is named in the Quran in Ali 'Imran 3:37 and Al-An'am 6:85. Some Muslims believe that he died a martyr.

christian.text: According to Christian scripture, Zechariah (Zakariya in the Islamic tradition), a venerable priest of the division of Abijah, lived with his wife Elizabeth in Judea. Both were righteous before God, diligently observing all the Lord's commands and decrees, though they were advanced in years and Elizabeth was barren. While Zechariah was serving in the temple, performing his priestly duties by offering incense, the angel Gabriel appeared to him. Gabriel announced that Elizabeth would miraculously conceive a son, whom they were to name John, and that he would be great in the sight of the Lord, preparing the way for the Messiah. Overwhelmed with doubt due to their old age, Zechariah questioned the angel's words. As a consequence for his disbelief, Gabriel declared that Zechariah would be unable to speak until the day these things happened. Indeed, he remained mute until John's birth. When the child was eight days old, the still-silent Zechariah wrote on a tablet, "His name is John." Immediately, his mouth opened, and his tongue was loosed, and he began to speak, praising God. Filled with the Holy Spirit, Zechariah then uttered a profound prophecy, recorded in the Gospel of Luke (Luke 1:68–79), known as the Benedictus, which glorified God and foretold John’s crucial role as a prophet who would prepare the way for the Lord and announce salvation through the forgiveness of sins.

jewish.text: Zechariah (Zakariya in the Islamic tradition), the father of John the Baptist (Yahya), is not a figure of the Hebrew Bible. His story is told in Christian scripture (the Gospel of Luke, chapter 1) — where he appears as a priest of the division of Abijah serving in the Jerusalem Temple — and in the Quran. Jewish scripture and classical rabbinic literature contain no account of him, though as a Temple priest of the late Second Temple period he would have belonged to the priestly divisions described in Jewish sources. He should not be confused with the biblical prophet Zechariah son of Berechiah, author of the Book of Zechariah, who lived some five centuries earlier during the rebuilding of the Second Temple; that earlier Zechariah's book is part of the Tanakh, while the father of John the Baptist is known only from later, non-Jewish sources.
sources: Bible, Gospel of Luke 1 (Christian scripture); Tanakh, Book of Zechariah (the distinct earlier prophet)

islamic.text: Prophet Yahya (John), peace be upon him, was the miraculously born son of Prophet Zakariyya. When Zakariyya had grown old and his wife was barren, he prayed to his Lord for an heir (Maryam 19:2–6; Ali 'Imran 3:38). While he stood praying in the sanctuary (mihrab), the angels called to him with glad tidings of Yahya, "confirming a word from Allah", honourable, abstaining from women, and a prophet from among the righteous (3:39). The Quran adds that no one before him had been given this name (19:7). When Zakariyya asked how he could have a son, he was told that it was easy for Allah, and as a sign he could not speak to people for three days except by gesture (3:40–41; 19:8–11). In another passage Allah says that He answered Zakariyya, gave him Yahya and made his wife fit for him, and that they hastened to good deeds and called on Allah in hope and fear (Al-Anbiya 21:89–90). Allah addressed him: "O Yahya, take the Scripture with determination." He was given judgement while still a boy, along with affection and purity from Allah; he was God-fearing and dutiful to his parents, and he was neither arrogant nor disobedient (19:12–14). The Quran concludes: "Peace be upon him the day he was born and the day he dies and the day he is raised alive" (19:15). He is also named with Zakariyya, Isa (Jesus) and Ilyas among the righteous (Al-An'am 6:85). In a hadith recorded by al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad describes meeting Yahya and Isa in the second heaven during his ascension (Mi'raj), and says that the two were maternal cousins (Sahih al-Bukhari 3887). According to tradition, Yahya died a martyr for fearlessly upholding Allah's commands against injustice.
sources: THE-O summary from sources: Qur'an 19:2–15, 3:37–41, 21:89–90, 6:85 (Saheeh International, https://api.alquran.cloud/v1/surah/19/en.sahih)

christian.text: John the Baptist (Yahya in the Islamic tradition), recognized in the Christian tradition as the divinely appointed forerunner to Jesus Christ, has his life extensively chronicled in the Gospels of the Christian Bible. His miraculous birth to the elderly priest Zechariah and his wife Elizabeth, a kinswoman of Mary, was announced by the angel Gabriel, who declared he would be filled with the Holy Spirit from birth and prepare a people for the Lord. John lived an austere life in the wilderness, dressed in camel hair with a leather belt and sustained by locusts and wild honey, embodying the ancient prophets. He emerged preaching a powerful message of repentance, urging people to turn from their sins and be baptized in the Jordan River in anticipation of the Messiah. John humbly proclaimed himself merely a voice crying out, announcing the imminent arrival of one greater than he, who would baptize with the Holy Spirit. His pivotal moment came when he baptized Jesus in the Jordan, witnessing the Holy Spirit descend like a dove and hearing a voice from heaven affirm Jesus as God’s beloved Son. John faithfully testified to Jesus as the "Lamb of God." His unwavering righteousness led him to publicly condemn Herod Antipas’s unlawful marriage to Herodias, resulting in his imprisonment. Ultimately, at Herodias’s vengeful demand, John was tragically beheaded, becoming a martyr for his prophetic witness and unwavering truth.

jewish.text: John the Baptist (Yahya in the Islamic tradition) does not appear in the Hebrew Bible or in classical rabbinic literature — he lived in the first century CE, after the books of the Tanakh were complete. The principal Jewish source about him is the first-century Jewish historian Flavius Josephus (Antiquities of the Jews 18.5.2), who describes John as a good man who commanded the Jews to exercise virtue, righteousness towards one another and piety towards God, and to join in baptism. Josephus relates that Herod Antipas, fearing that John's great influence over the people might lead to an uprising, had him imprisoned and put to death at the fortress of Machaerus. Historians value Josephus's account as independent, non-Christian evidence for John's life and death; it presents him simply as a righteous Jewish preacher of his time.

islamic.text: Prophet Isa ibn Maryam (Jesus son of Mary), peace be upon him, is one of the most revered prophets and messengers in Islam and the Messiah (al-Masih) sent to the Children of Israel. He is named in 25 verses of the Quran, more often than the Prophet Muhammad, among them Al-Baqarah 2:87, and his mother Maryam (Mary) is the only woman named in the Quran; Surah Maryam bears her name. His birth is a sign from Allah: he was born to the virgin Maryam without a father, brought into being by Allah's command, "Be!" and it is (Ali 'Imran 3:42–47; Maryam 19:16–36). The Quran calls him a Word of Allah delivered to Maryam and a spirit from Him (An-Nisa 4:171). As an infant in the cradle he spoke to defend his mother's honour, declaring himself a servant and prophet of Allah, not a divine being or a son of God; Islam rejects the Trinity and divine sonship. He brought the Injil (Gospel), which confirmed the Tawrah before it, and called people to worship Allah alone; Muslims hold that this original message was later altered. By Allah's permission (bi-idhni-llah) he fashioned birds from clay and breathed life into them, healed the blind and the leper, and raised the dead (Ali 'Imran 3:45–55; Al-Ma'idah 5:110). He foretold the coming of the Prophet Muhammad after him (As-Saff 61:6). The Quran states that he was not crucified: "they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it appeared so to them," and Allah raised him to Himself (An-Nisa 4:157–158). Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi record several views of what happened, the dominant one being that another was made to resemble him. Based on hadith reports, including in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, mainstream Muslims believe Isa is alive and will return before the Day of Judgement: he will descend at the white minaret in Damascus, kill the Dajjal (Antichrist), break the cross, kill the swine and establish justice, then die a natural death; some reports add that he will be buried beside the Prophet Muhammad in Medina. Some scholars, however, hold that the Quran itself does not mention a second coming.

christian.text: According to Christian belief, Jesus (Isa in the Islamic tradition), central to the Christian faith, is revered as the Son of God and the Messiah, prophesied in the Old Testament. His life, detailed in the four Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John) of the Holy Bible, begins with his miraculous birth in Bethlehem to the Virgin Mary, conceived by the Holy Spirit. Fully God and fully man, Jesus lived a sinless life, demonstrating perfect obedience to God. His public ministry was marked by profound teachings, parables, miraculous healings, and casting out demons, all revealing God's love and power. He called humanity to repentance and faith in the Kingdom of God. Ultimately, Jesus willingly offered himself as a sacrifice for the sins of the world, suffering crucifixion under Pontius Pilate in Jerusalem. Christian belief affirms that on the third day, God raised him from the dead, triumphing over sin and death. After appearing to many disciples, Jesus ascended into heaven, where he now sits at the right hand of God the Father. Christians await his promised second coming to judge the living and the dead and establish his eternal kingdom. The Bible stands as the inspired word of God, providing the foundational truths of Jesus' life, death, and resurrection, which are essential to salvation.
sources: Bible, Gospels of Matthew, Mark, Luke, John

jewish.text: Jesus (called Isa in the Islamic tradition) was a Jewish man who lived in Judea during the period of Roman rule. Later rabbinic writings and historical accounts acknowledge his existence as a figure who gathered followers. During his time, he was understood by some to present himself as the awaited Messiah. However, from a Jewish perspective, the criteria for the Messiah, as meticulously detailed within the Tanakh — which includes the Torah, Prophets, and Writings — were not fulfilled by Jesus. Jewish tradition teaches that the Messiah will be a human leader, a descendant of King David, who will rebuild the Holy Temple in Jerusalem, gather all exiled Jews back to the Land of Israel, and usher in a universal era of peace and complete knowledge of God. This messianic age is characterized by global adherence to the ethical and legal teachings of the Torah, eliminating war and suffering. Jesus did not bring about these transformative events, nor did his actions align with the prophetic expectations. Consequently, his claims were rejected by the Jewish religious leadership and the majority of the Jewish people of his era. He was ultimately executed by the Roman authorities, likely for perceived sedition or claims of kingship which threatened Roman sovereignty. Within Judaism, Jesus is not considered a prophet, nor is his death understood to possess any redemptive power. Jewish theology maintains the absolute oneness of God and the everlasting validity of the Torah, without requiring a divine intermediary or sacrifice for sin.
sources: Tanakh (messianic criteria); later rabbinic and historical sources

bahai.text: Isa, revered in the Baháʼí Faith as a mighty Manifestation of God, appeared in Palestine to inaugurate a new and glorious dispensation of divine guidance. Born of the Virgin Mary through miraculous power, He lived a life of profound purity, selfless devotion, and exemplary servitude. His profound teachings, recorded in the Gospels (Injíl) and elucidated by Baháʼí sacred texts, illuminated the path of love, compassion, justice, and the establishment of the Kingdom of God on earth. Isa proclaimed the oneness of God and the inherent unity of humanity, calling all to spiritual transformation and reconciliation. Through His divinely revealed words and wondrous deeds, He unveiled eternal truths, healed the sick, and offered hope to the despairing, emphasizing the spirit of sacrifice and service. He endured immense suffering and was ultimately crucified, an event affirmed in Baháʼí writings as a profound testament to His mission. Yet, His sacred Spirit ascended, and His advent, along with other Manifestations, prepared humanity for the eventual advent of Baháʼu'lláh, who fulfills the prophecies of His return and brings to fruition the spiritual springtime initiated by Isa, guiding humanity towards its collective maturity and the establishment of global peace.

islamic.text: Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, the son of Abdullah ibn Abd al-Muttalib and Amina bint Wahb, was born in Makkah (Mecca) around 570 CE, the Year of the Elephant, into the Banu Hashim clan of the Quraysh. His father died around the time of his birth and his mother when he was six, and the orphan was raised by his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib and then his uncle Abu Talib. Known for his truthfulness and integrity, he was given the title al-Amin (the Trustworthy). He would retreat for nights of prayer to the cave of Hira, and there, at the age of forty, around 610 CE, the angel Jibril (Gabriel) brought him the first revelation from Allah. From 613 he preached openly that Allah is One and that complete submission (Islam) to Him is the right way of life. His followers, few at first, suffered persecution by the Meccans for thirteen years; in 615 he sent some of them to Abyssinia, and in 622 he and his followers migrated to Medina, then called Yathrib. This Hijra marks the start of the Islamic calendar. In Medina he established the first Muslim community and united the tribes under the Constitution of Medina. After eight years of intermittent fighting with the Meccan tribes, he marched on Makkah with 10,000 Muslims and took the city largely unopposed, with few casualties. He completed his mission with the Farewell Pilgrimage; a few months later he fell ill and died in Medina on 8 June 632 CE, by which time most of the Arabian Peninsula had accepted Islam. The Quran says, "Muhammad is no more than a messenger; other messengers have gone before him" (Ali 'Imran 3:144), and calls him "the Messenger of Allah and the seal of the prophets" (Al-Ahzab 33:40). Muslims believe he is the last messenger, sent by Allah to all of humanity to confirm the message of one God brought by Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Isa and the other prophets. The revelations he received form the verses of the Quran, which Muslims hold to be the word of Allah, and his Sunnah, his teachings and example preserved in the hadith and the sira, is a source of Islamic law.

bahai.text: Muhammad, the Prophet of Islam, is revered in the Bahá'í Faith as a divinely appointed Manifestation of God, a luminary in the eternal succession of Divine Messengers sent to humanity. He appeared in seventh-century Arabia, a land then steeped in idolatry and moral decline, to rekindle the light of God's oneness and establish a new spiritual dispensation. Through Him, God revealed the Holy Qur’án, a sacred scripture containing laws, spiritual truths, and prophecies that profoundly reshaped human understanding and governance. He called people to worship the one true God, advocating for justice, charity, and brotherhood, and to abandon polytheism and corrupt practices. His profound message was met with fierce opposition from those attached to old traditions, leading to His historic migration, known as the Hijra, from Mecca to Medina. There, He established a nascent community dedicated to God’s teachings, demonstrating principles of unity and spiritual governance. Despite immense challenges and persecution, Muhammad tirelessly proclaimed the divine message, inspiring a profound transformation that unified disparate tribes under the banner of Islam and laid the foundations for a vast civilization. Bahá'ís recognize Him as a vital link in the unbroken chain of Progressive Revelation, perfectly fulfilling the prophecies of previous dispensations and preparing the way for future Manifestations, including the Báb and Bahá’u’lláh, all reflecting the one indivisible Light of God.
